messages.content: When a speaker plays a note, is the air itself traveling from the speaker to my ear?

No — and the distinction is the whole idea of a wave. What travels is a pattern of pressure, not the air. Each air molecule just shuffles a tiny distance back and forth around its resting place: pushed forward where the wave compresses the air, drifting back where the wave rarefies it. A molecule near the speaker never makes the trip to your ear; it hands the push to its neighbor, which hands it on, the way a stadium wave travels around the stands while every fan stays in their seat. That is why sound is not a wind. A candle flame in front of a woofer flickers because the pressure at that spot is oscillating, not because a steady breeze is blowing it over. The energy makes the journey — at about 343 meters per second in room-temperature air — while the matter stays home, oscillating. One honest caveat: at very high intensities the tidy picture bends a little (the wave steepens and the motion is no longer perfectly symmetric), but for every sound you will ever hear in a room, energy travels and air does not.
Why does every octave on a piano sound like 'the same note, higher'? And how much does the frequency actually change across the keyboard?

Because an octave is not a step, it is a doubling. Pitch perception tracks ratios, so the note one octave up always has exactly twice the frequency — that constant ratio is what your ear hears as 'the same note, lifted.' Watch the doublings accumulate from the piano's lowest A, 27.5 Hz, over seven octaves:
Seven doublings give 3520 Hz — the A seven octaves up, and the keyboard's top C sits just beyond it near 4,186 Hz. The same rule at the middle of the keyboard, doubling middle C:

523.26 Hz is the C above middle C. The striking part is the asymmetry the doublings create: the bottom octave of the piano spans only about 27 Hz of frequency, while the top octave spans over 2,000 Hz — yet they feel like equal steps, because hearing is a ratio instrument, not a ruler.
How big is a sound wave, actually? Like, physically how long?

It depends entirely on the frequency, because wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency: λ = v/f. At the very bottom of human hearing, 20 Hz — the territory elephants also use to rumble to each other across savanna:
One wave is 17.15 meters long — longer than a bus. At the top of a young ear's range, 20,000 Hz, up where bats hunt:

The same formula gives 1.71 centimeters — a wave smaller than a thumbnail. This size difference explains a lot of everyday acoustics. The 17-meter wave bends around houses and flows through doorways almost as if they were not there, which is why the bass from a party reaches you streets away. The centimeter-scale wave is easily blocked, reflected, and shadowed, which is why the words and sparkle of that same party vanish behind the first wall. Big waves go around things; small waves bounce off them.
Does sound really travel faster on a warm day? By how much?

It does, and the rule of thumb is simple: the speed of sound in air rises by about 0.6 meters per second for every degree Celsius of warming, starting from about 331 m/s at freezing. A mild room-temperature day at 20 °C:
That gives 343 m/s, the familiar figure. A hot afternoon at 35 °C:

Now 352 m/s — about 3 percent faster than at 20 °C. The mechanism is molecular: warmer air means faster-moving molecules, and a pressure disturbance is passed along by molecular collisions, so the hand-off itself speeds up. (Density is not the driver here — hot air is less dense, yet sound goes faster, because molecular speed wins.) The effect is small enough to ignore for thunder-counting, but orchestras notice it: a wind instrument's pitch is set by the speed of sound in its tube, so a cold hall literally makes the flutes flat until the air inside them warms up.
Count the seconds between lightning and thunder, divide by three, and that's kilometers away. Does that rule actually work?

It works surprisingly well, and it is worth seeing why. Sound needs time to cross the distance; light effectively does not — the flash arrives within microseconds. Suppose you count 6 seconds. At 343 m/s the sound has covered:
2058 meters, so the storm is about 2.06 km off. The folk rule says 6 divided by 3 is 2 km. The error in that shortcut:

Roughly 2.8 percent — the rule is good to within a few percent, because 343 m/s is close to a third of a kilometer per second. The honest limits: the rule measures the distance to the nearest part of the lightning channel, which can be a long, branching bolt, so 'the storm' may not be a single point; wind and temperature gradients bend sound and can muffle a distant strike entirely; and the count only ever tells you distance, never direction of travel. For direction you need two counts, minutes apart — a shrinking gap means the storm is coming closer, which is the part that actually matters for safety.
If a singer holds a note and just sings it louder, why doesn't the pitch go up?

Because pitch and loudness live on different axes of the wave, and your ear reads them separately. Pitch is set by frequency — how many pressure cycles arrive per second — and that is fixed by how fast the vocal folds are vibrating. Loudness is set by amplitude — how far the pressure swings above and below atmospheric in each cycle. Singing louder means driving the same vibration harder: more air pressure behind each cycle, bigger swings, same number of cycles per second. Think of a jump rope: you can swing it in big wide arcs or small tight ones at exactly the same rhythm. The rope's speed is the frequency; the width of the arcs is the amplitude. A third axis completes the picture — timbre, the recipe of overtones riding on the fundamental, which is why the same note at the same loudness still sounds different from a flute and from a violin. Three independent knobs: frequency for pitch, amplitude for loudness, spectrum for color. Mixing up the first two is natural in everyday language ('turn it up' means louder, not higher), but the physics keeps them cleanly apart.
Why is there no sound in space? And why does sound travel faster underwater if water is 'thicker'?

Sound is a mechanical wave: it is nothing but organized pushing between neighboring particles, so where there are no particles there is nothing to push. Space is a near-perfect vacuum — a few atoms per cubic centimeter against the roughly 10^19 molecules in every cubic centimeter of air — so a pressure pattern has no medium to propagate through. Explosions in space really would be silent to any ear or microphone floating nearby. Water is the opposite lesson. Sound crosses water at about 1,480 m/s, more than four times faster than in air, and steel carries it near 5,000 m/s. That seems backwards until you separate the two properties that set wave speed: stiffness and density. Density slows a wave down, but stiffness — how violently the material pushes back when compressed — speeds it up, and in water and steel the stiffness grows far more than the density does. Water is nearly incompressible, so a squeeze at one point is transmitted almost instantly to the next layer. Air is a soft spring; water is a stiff one. Speed of sound is really a measurement of how stiff the medium is for its weight.
How long does one cycle of a 440 Hz tone last? It feels instant.
The period is the reciprocal of the frequency — one divided by 440, converted to milliseconds:

Each cycle of concert A lasts 2.27 milliseconds. Your eardrum is being pushed in and out 440 times a second, and the auditory system resolves the individual timing well enough to extract pitch from it. Compare the low hum of mains electricity at 50 Hz:

A full 20 milliseconds per cycle — nearly ten times slower, which is part of why deep bass feels more like a sequence of pulses or a physical pressure than a clean tone, and why rhythm itself lives down at these timescales: a drumbeat at two per second is a 2 Hz phenomenon, far below pitch, in the territory the brain handles as events in time rather than as sound quality.
How much does the air pressure actually change when a loud sound passes? I imagine it's a lot.

It is startlingly little, and checking the fraction makes the ear's sensitivity vivid. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101,325 pascals. A sound at the edge of discomfort, around 120 dB, has a pressure amplitude of roughly 20 pascals. As a percentage of the air pressure already pressing on you:

About 0.02 percent. The loudest sound you can tolerate is a wobble of a few hundredths of one percent in the ambient pressure — and at the threshold of hearing the wobble is a million times smaller still, around 20 micropascals. The displacements are just as extreme: at threshold, the eardrum and the air molecules move by roughly 10^-11 meters, on the order of the diameter of a single atom. Hearing is not a rugged sense measuring big forces; it is an exquisitely amplified instrument for detecting almost-nothing, which is precisely why it needs the mechanical amplification machinery of the middle ear to work at all.
My piano tuner listens for a slow 'wah-wah-wah' when two notes are almost in tune. What is that?

Those are beats, and they are arithmetic you can hear. When two tones of slightly different frequency sound together, they drift in and out of phase: where their peaks align they reinforce, half a cycle of drift later they cancel. The loudness pulses at the difference of the two frequencies. For a string at 442 Hz sounded against a 440 Hz reference:

The pulsing comes 2 times per second — slow enough to count. As the tuner brings the string toward 440, the difference shrinks and the wah-wah stretches out: one pulse every two seconds means the string is within half a hertz. At exact unison the beats vanish, which is a far more precise test than judging pitch directly — the ear can hear a beat slower than one per second, certifying agreement to a fraction of a hertz. The same effect, unwanted, is why two slightly detuned instruments playing together sound sour and restless: a flute at 663 Hz against strings at 660 gives:
3 shimmering pulses per second layered over the chord. Beats are a nuisance in an orchestra and a precision instrument on the workbench — the physics is identical.
Why do we need a weird logarithmic scale for sound at all? Why not just measure the power?

Because the honest numbers are unusable. The faintest sound a young ear can detect carries an intensity of about 10^-12 watts per square meter. Sound at the threshold of pain is around 1 watt per square meter. The ratio between barely-anything and too-much:

A trillion to one — 1000000000000. No linear scale survives a range like that: everything you care about (whispers, voices, music) would be crushed into the bottom sliver. The decibel compresses the trillion into something pocket-sized by counting powers of ten: every factor of ten in intensity is one 'bel', ten decibels. The trillion becomes:

120 decibels — the familiar 0-to-120-and-something range of hearing charts. The logarithm is not a bureaucratic complication; it is the only kind of ruler that fits the phenomenon. As a bonus, it roughly matches perception, because the ear itself responds to ratios more than to absolute differences.
People say '+10 dB is ten times more powerful but only sounds twice as loud.' Both halves can't be true... can they?

Both halves are true, because they describe two different quantities. The first half is the scale's definition: +10 dB always means exactly ten times the intensity. Take a sound a thousand times above the hearing threshold:

Its intensity is 1000.0000000000001 times the threshold intensity, three factors of ten, so it sits at 30 dB — a quiet whisper's neighborhood. That arithmetic is exact. The second half is about perception, and it is a rule of thumb rather than a law: in listening experiments, people asked to pick a sound 'twice as loud' as a reference typically land near +10 dB, across a broad middle range of levels and frequencies. So the chain runs: +10 dB = 10× the physical intensity ≈ 2× the perceived loudness; +20 dB = 100× the intensity ≈ 4× as loud. The approximation frays at very low and very high levels and varies between listeners, which is why careful writers say 'roughly twice as loud.' But as a pocket conversion for everyday sounds, it holds up well — and it explains why amplifier watts are so misleading: doubling your amplifier power buys only +3 dB, a clearly noticeable step, not a doubling of loudness.
If one machine is 80 dB, are two machines 160 dB?

No — decibels do not add like that, because they are logarithms. What adds is intensity: two independent machines pour twice the acoustic power into the room. Twice the intensity, expressed in decibels, is 10 × log10(2) — and log10(2) is almost exactly 0.3, which the calculator confirms from the other direction:

10^0.3 ≈ 2, a doubling. So doubling intensity adds just 3 dB: two 80 dB machines together make about 83 dB, not 160. Gaining another 3 dB means doubling again — four machines for 86, eight for 89. This is the tyranny of the logarithm for anyone fighting noise: removing half the machines in a hall only buys 3 dB. It cuts the other way too — the first sound source in a silent room matters enormously, and each equal addition matters less. (One precision: this holds for independent, uncorrelated sources like separate machines. Two sources driven in perfect lockstep can interfere constructively and gain up to 6 dB where their waves align — a different phenomenon, and the reason paired loudspeakers behave specially.)
How much quieter does a sound get as I walk away from it?

In open air, intensity follows the inverse-square law: the same power spreads over a sphere whose area grows with the square of the distance, so doubling the distance quarters the intensity — and a factor of four in intensity is 6 dB. The cleanest case is stepping ten times farther away: intensity falls by a factor of:

100, exactly two powers of ten, so exactly 20 dB lost: a shout measuring 80 dB at 1 meter is about 60 dB at 10 meters, conversational level. The doubling version compounds quickly — going from 1 meter to 8 meters is three doublings, and the intensity ratio is:

A factor of 64 less intensity, roughly 18 dB down. Two honest caveats: this is the free-field law, outdoors or in anechoic conditions. Indoors, reflections off walls keep feeding energy back, so levels fall off more slowly with distance and eventually plateau into the room's reverberant field — which is why a shout carries across a gym far better than the inverse-square law alone predicts.
Give me the standard table of decibel levels for everyday sounds — and tell me how much to trust it.

Treat every number below as a typical value, not a measurement: levels depend on distance from the source, the exact source, and the room, so honest tables give ranges. With that warning, the usual reference points (dB SPL, measured near the source unless noted) are approximately:

- 0 dB — threshold of hearing for a young ear at its most sensitive frequency
- 10–20 dB — a quiet recording studio; rustling leaves
- 30 dB — a whisper at about a meter
- 40 dB — a quiet library or a calm residential room
- 60 dB — ordinary conversation at a meter
- 70 dB — a vacuum cleaner or a shower at close range
- 85 dB — heavy city traffic from the curb; the level where long daily exposure starts to matter for hearing
- 100 dB — a motorcycle or a factory machine at arm's length
- 110 dB — a rock concert near the speakers; a baby crying right at your ear
- 120 dB — the neighborhood of discomfort and pain for many listeners; a thunderclap overhead
- 130+ dB — a jet engine at close range

Two reading skills matter more than memorizing the table. First, a decibel figure without a distance is meaningless — the same vacuum cleaner is 70 dB at your hand and far less across the street. Second, the steps are not equal: the gap from 60 to 70 dB is ten times the intensity, and from 60 to 90 dB is a thousand times, even though the numbers look like a gentle staircase.
Why does hearing damage depend on both loudness and time? What's the actual trade-off?

Because the inner ear is damaged by dose — total acoustic energy delivered — more than by any instant's level alone. The widely used occupational guideline (the NIOSH criterion) anchors the exchange at 85 dB for 8 hours, with a 3 dB exchange rate: every 3 dB louder halves the time that delivers the same dose, because 3 dB is a doubling of intensity. At 88 dB the same dose arrives in:
4 hours. At 94 dB:

Just 1 hour delivers the full day's dose — and the pattern continues brutally, down to minutes at concert-front levels. This is presented as general education about how the guideline works, not as a personal safety calculation: real standards differ in their anchor and exchange rate (some regulatory regimes use 90 dB and a 5 dB exchange), individual susceptibility varies, and brief peaks carry their own risks that a dose average hides. The durable insight is the shape of the trade: because the scale is logarithmic, small increases in level buy disproportionately large increases in energy, and time is the only currency you can pay less of.
Can a decibel level be negative? And why does my audio software show 0 dB as the maximum?

Yes to the first, and the second explains the confusion: a decibel is never an absolute amount — it is always a ratio to some reference, and the reference changes between fields. In acoustics, 0 dB SPL means 'equal to the reference pressure,' about 20 micropascals, chosen because it sits near the average young ear's threshold. It does not mean no sound. Sounds weaker than the reference simply score negative, and the quietest rooms on Earth — anechoic chambers — genuinely measure around −10 to −20 dBA; in them you hear your own heartbeat and blood flow. Your audio software uses a completely different reference: 0 dBFS means 'full scale,' the largest value the digital system can represent. There, 0 is a ceiling, everything real is below it, and all readings are negative by construction. Electrical engineering has its own references again (dBV, dBu, referenced to specific voltages). So the same word names at least three different rulers. Whenever a decibel figure matters, the first question is 'relative to what?' — a number without its reference is a length without units.
My neighbor's TV is 70 dB and mine is 80 dB. Through the wall, do I hear 150 dB of combined TV?

You hear something much less dramatic, and the arithmetic shows why the louder source nearly always wins. Levels cannot be added, but intensities can. In units of the hearing threshold, an 80 dB sound has intensity 10^8 and a 70 dB sound 10^7. Their sum:
110000000 — and compared with the louder source alone:

Only 1.1 times its intensity, which on the decibel scale is about 80.4 dB total. The 70 dB television, a full ten decibels down, contributes a mere 0.4 dB to the combination. The practical moral cuts two ways. If you are trying to quiet a space, silencing the second-loudest source gains almost nothing until the loudest is dealt with. And if a measurement rises slightly when something switches on, the newcomer may be far quieter than the background it joined. Decibel addition is dominated-source arithmetic: near-equal sources add their famous 3 dB, but a source 10 dB down is nearly a spectator.
Why does the bass on my stereo seem to disappear when I turn the volume down?

Because your ear's sensitivity is not flat, and its unevenness changes with level. The ear is most sensitive in the 2–5 kHz region — roughly the band of speech clarity and, not coincidentally, of the ear canal's own resonance — and markedly less sensitive to deep bass and extreme treble. Crucially, that insensitivity is worst at low listening levels. At concert volume, a 50 Hz tone and a 1 kHz tone at the same measured level sound roughly comparable in loudness; turn everything down 40 dB and the bass tone fades toward inaudibility while the midrange is still clearly present. These are the equal-loudness contours, mapped by Fletcher and Munson in the 1930s and refined since. The music did not change; your receiver's frequency response did. Older amplifiers had a 'loudness' button that boosted bass and treble at low volumes precisely to compensate for your ear, and modern systems do the same trick automatically. It is also why a mix balanced at high volume sounds thin and midrange-heavy when played quietly — engineers know to check their work at low level, where the ear's curve does its worst.
A jet at takeoff is about 130 dB and conversation is 60 dB. How much more intense is the jet, really?
The gap is 70 dB, and every 10 dB is a factor of ten in intensity, so the ratio is ten to the seventh:

The jet delivers 10000000 — ten million — times the intensity of conversation at those measurement points. Now translate that into perception using the rule of thumb that each 10 dB roughly doubles perceived loudness. Seventy decibels is seven such steps:

2^7 = 128: the jet sounds on the order of a hundred-odd times louder, not ten million times. That compression is the ear's great design compromise — it squeezes a trillion-fold physical range into a manageable perceptual range — and it is exactly why our intuitions fail so badly around sound. Numbers that look close on the decibel scale (60 versus 130) are worlds apart in energy, while differences that feel modest ('twice as loud') hide tenfold physical jumps. When someone says a noise is 'only a few decibels more,' the honest translation is: a few decibels is a doubling or halving of power, every time.
Walk me through what actually happens between a sound hitting my ear and me hearing it.

The ear is three machines in series, each solving a different problem. The outer ear is the collector: the pinna funnels sound into the canal and, by the way it shadows and reflects different frequencies, tags sounds with direction clues; the canal is a short tube that happens to resonate in the speech-clarity band, giving those frequencies a free boost before anything else happens. The middle ear is the transmission: the eardrum vibrates, and three tiny bones — malleus, incus, stapes, the smallest bones in the body — carry that vibration to the oval window of the inner ear, transforming it on the way from large, weak movements in air to small, forceful ones suited to fluid. The inner ear is the analyzer and transducer: inside the coiled cochlea, the fluid wave sets a membrane rippling, hair cells bend, and mechanical motion becomes electrochemical signal — thousands of separate frequency channels reporting up the auditory nerve in parallel. Collection, impedance-matching, analysis. Most hearing problems can be located by asking which of the three machines is failing, which is why clinicians distinguish conductive losses (the first two machines) from sensorineural ones (the third).
Why do we need those three little bones at all? Why can't the eardrum just push on the fluid directly?

Because air and fluid refuse to cooperate. Sound in air is a large, feeble pressure wobble; the cochlea is filled with fluid, which is stiff and dense. If airborne sound struck the cochlear fluid directly, on the order of 99.9 percent of its energy would simply reflect off the surface — the same reason you can barely hear someone shouting at you from above the water when you are submerged. The ossicles are a pressure transformer that fixes the mismatch. The eardrum's effective area is about 55 square millimeters; the stapes footplate that drives the fluid is about 3.2. The area ratio:
Collecting the eardrum's force onto a spot 17.2 times smaller multiplies the pressure by that factor. The bone chain also works as a lever with a ratio near 1.3, adding its own gain:

Total pressure gain, roughly 22.4-fold — in decibel terms, the high twenties of dB of free amplification, almost exactly canceling the air-to-fluid penalty. It is the same trick as a thumbtack: spread your thumb's push over its wide head, deliver it through the pin's tiny point, and the pressure at the tip is enormous. Evolution built a thumbtack into your head.
How does the cochlea separate a chord into individual notes? There's no little piano in there... is there?

Functionally, there almost is — a keyboard laid out in a spiral, played by waves. The cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube divided along its length by the basilar membrane, and that membrane is not uniform: near the base of the coil it is narrow and stiff; toward the apex it is wider and floppier. When the stapes pumps the fluid, a traveling wave runs along the membrane, and where it peaks depends on frequency. High frequencies peak almost immediately, near the stiff base; low frequencies travel the whole coil and peak at the loose apex. So frequency is converted into place: each spot on the membrane reports, in effect, 'energy at my frequency arrived.' Rows of hair cells along the membrane transduce their local motion, and the auditory nerve carries thousands of these place-labeled channels to the brain — a spectrum analysis performed by plumbing. This is called place theory, and it explains a great deal: why hearing loss often eats specific frequency bands (one stretch of membrane wears out), and why a cochlear implant can restore a usable sense of pitch by stimulating different positions along the coil with different channels of a processed signal.
What do hair cells actually do, and why does everyone say they don't grow back?

Hair cells are the moment of conversion — the place where mechanics becomes electricity. Each carries a tuft of fine bristles (stereocilia) linked by tiny filaments. When the basilar membrane ripples, the tuft bends, the filaments tug open ion channels, and the cell fires off a chemical signal to the auditory nerve. Two populations divide the work. The inner hair cells — a single row of about 3,500 per ear — are the true sensors; nearly all the nerve fibers listen to them. The outer hair cells, three rows of about 12,000, are stranger: they are amplifiers. They physically change length in response to voltage, dancing in time with the incoming wave and pumping energy back into the membrane's motion. That active feedback is what gives hearing its astonishing sensitivity and sharp frequency tuning — it can add the equivalent of tens of decibels of gain for quiet sounds. The 'don't grow back' part is, for mammals, essentially accurate as general biology: birds and fish regenerate hair cells, but the mammalian cochlea does not replace them once they die, so losses from noise, aging, and some medicines accumulate over a lifetime. That asymmetry — a regenerative design in other lineages, a fixed endowment in ours — is one reason hearing conservation advice is so emphatic, and why the cochlea's amplifier cells, working hardest, tend to fail first.
Why do my ears pop on a plane, and why does swallowing help?

Behind your eardrum is the sealed-ish cavity of the middle ear, and its pressure needs to match the outside world for the eardrum to sit at rest and vibrate freely. The matching is done by the Eustachian tube, a narrow passage from the middle ear to the back of the throat, normally closed and opening briefly when you swallow, yawn, or chew. On a climb, cabin pressure falls; the middle ear's trapped air expands and usually vents passively with little drama. Descent is the troublesome direction: outside pressure rises, the eardrum is pushed inward, and the tube — which acts a bit like a one-way valve — resists letting air back in, so you feel fullness, muffled hearing, and sometimes pain until it yields. Swallowing works because the same throat muscles that move food also tug the tube open, letting the pressures equalize with that familiar pop, which is simply the eardrum snapping back to its neutral position. Congestion makes it worse for a mechanical reason: swollen tissue narrows the tube further. It is plumbing, not damage — a pressure-equalization valve doing a job that only becomes noticeable when the pressure around you changes faster than the valve likes to open.
Why does my voice sound so weird and thin on recordings? That's not how I sound.

It is exactly how you sound — to everyone else. The discrepancy is a missing transmission path. When you speak, your cochlea receives your voice by two routes at once. The first is the ordinary air route: sound leaves your mouth, curves around, and enters your ear canal, the same path everyone else hears. The second is bone conduction: the vibrations of your vocal folds shake the tissues and bones of your skull directly, and that shaking reaches the cochlea from inside. Bone and tissue transmit low frequencies especially efficiently, so the voice you are used to is your air-conducted voice enriched with a private bass feed that no one else receives. A recording captures only the air route. Played back, the familiar low warmth is absent, and the voice sounds thinner and higher — not because the recording is lying, but because it is missing a channel you have heard your whole life. Microphones have no skulls. This is also why the effect never fades for most people: every day of speaking refreshes the bone-conducted version, so the recording always sounds like a stranger by comparison.
Is it a coincidence that human hearing is most sensitive right in the frequency band of speech?

Part of the answer is sitting in your head: the ear canal is itself a resonator that amplifies exactly that band. The canal is a tube roughly 2.5 centimeters long, open at one end and closed at the eardrum. A tube like that resonates at the frequency whose wavelength is four times the tube's length. That frequency:

3430 Hz — about 3.4 kHz, squarely inside the 2–5 kHz region where hearing thresholds are lowest and where the consonant sounds that carry speech intelligibility live. The canal's resonance contributes on the order of 10 dB of free gain there. Whether to call it coincidence or co-evolution is a deeper question: speech evolved in ears that already had this shape, and the frequencies that matter most for distinguishing 'sa' from 'fa' sit where the hardware hears best. Either way, the match between the speech band and the sensitivity peak is not an accident of the threshold curve alone — a simple tube of flesh and cartilage is doing quiet acoustic engineering before the sound ever reaches the eardrum.
How do my ears tell where a sound is coming from? The timing differences must be microscopic.

They are, and the brain measures them anyway. A sound arriving from your right reaches the right ear first. The extra distance to the far ear is at most the width of your head — take about 18 centimeters of effective path difference for a sound directly to one side:

The far ear is delayed by at most about 0.52 milliseconds — half a millisecond — yet listeners can use interaural time differences of a few tens of microseconds, a small fraction of that maximum, to place a sound within a degree or two. Time cues work best for low frequencies, whose waves are long enough that the phase difference between the ears is unambiguous. For high frequencies the head casts a genuine sound shadow, so the far ear receives a measurably quieter signal, and the brain switches to that level difference. The two systems overlap in the middle frequencies. Front-versus-back and up-versus-down cannot be solved by either cue — sounds on the 'cone of confusion' produce identical timing and level pairs — and there the pinna earns its keep: its folds filter frequencies differently depending on the sound's elevation and front-back position, and the brain reads those spectral fingerprints. It is also why a small head movement resolves confusion instantly: turning changes all the cues in a pattern only one true direction can explain.
Is there really a reflex that protects the ear from loud sounds? Why doesn't it save us from gunshots, then?

There is — the acoustic reflex. When intense sound arrives, a small muscle called the stapedius contracts and stiffens the stapes, the last bone in the middle-ear chain, bracing the transmission line and reducing how much low-frequency energy gets through to the cochlea. A second muscle tenses the eardrum itself. The reflex is real and useful: it engages during sustained loud sound, it activates just before you speak or chew (which is why your own voice and your own chewing don't deafen you), and it preferentially damps low frequencies, which slightly improves speech clarity in noise. Its fatal limitation is speed. The reflex takes tens of milliseconds to engage — fast for a muscle, hopeless against a gunshot or a firecracker, whose damaging peak is over in a fraction of a millisecond, long before any contraction begins. It also fatigues, relaxing its guard during minutes of continuous loud sound. So the reflex is best understood as protection against the sounds of your own body and a modest buffer against sustained noise, not armor against impulses. The honest summary: evolution gave the ear a volume knob with a slow hand, well matched to a pre-industrial soundscape of voices, weather, and animals — and badly outpaced by explosives.
Why do ear problems sometimes make people dizzy? What does balance have to do with hearing?

They share a building. The inner ear houses two instruments in one fluid-filled labyrinth: the cochlea for hearing, and right beside it the vestibular system for balance — three semicircular canals that sense rotation of the head, plus two small organs (the utricle and saccule) that sense linear acceleration and gravity's direction. The semicircular canals work elegantly: each is a fluid ring oriented in a different plane, and when the head rotates, the fluid lags behind, bending hair cells that report the rotation. Because the two systems are neighbors sharing fluid spaces, membranes, and a nerve bundle, trouble in one often spills into the other. An inner-ear infection can inflame both; the pressure disorder Ménière's disease classically produces vertigo attacks together with fluctuating hearing and tinnitus in the same ear; even an intense low-frequency sound can slosh the vestibular organs, a curiosity called the Tullio phenomenon. The pairing is not a design flaw so much as a shared ancestry — both organs evolved from the same hair-cell technology, packaged together in the densest bone in the body. When a clinician hears 'dizzy with ear symptoms,' the shared plumbing is exactly why they take the combination seriously. (That is general anatomy, not an assessment of any particular case of dizziness, which has many possible causes.)
When I pluck a guitar string, I hear one note. You keep saying there are many frequencies in it. Show me.

A vibrating string does not move in just one pattern. It vibrates as a whole — the fundamental — and simultaneously in halves, thirds, quarters, each segment pattern adding its own tone at an exact multiple of the fundamental frequency. For the A string tuned to 110 Hz, the series runs 110, 220, 330, 440, 550, 660... The fifth harmonic:
550 Hz. The sixth:

660 Hz. These integer multiples are called harmonics, and they are not faint decorations — in a typical plucked note the first several harmonics carry much of the sound's energy, and the fundamental is sometimes not even the loudest component. Your ear fuses the whole stack into a single perceived pitch (the fundamental) plus a tone color (the recipe of the stack). The recipe is why instruments are distinguishable at all: a clarinet emphasizes odd harmonics, a bowed string produces a rich full ladder, and plucking the same string near its end versus its middle changes which harmonics get excited — the mellow-versus-bright difference guitarists exploit without ever naming the physics.
If a flute and a violin play the same note at the same loudness, what is physically different about the sounds?

Nearly everything except the fundamental frequency. A musical tone is a stack of harmonics, and the two instruments build very different stacks. A flute's air column produces a nearly pure tone — a strong fundamental with weak overtones, especially in its low register — which is why it sounds smooth, hollow, and 'simple.' A bowed violin string produces a dense ladder of harmonics extending high, driven by the bow's stick-slip grip, and the wooden body then filters that ladder through its own resonances, boosting some bands and swallowing others; the result is the bright, complex, slightly nasal signature you recognize instantly. Layered on top is the envelope: the flute's note swells in over tens of milliseconds, the violin's speaks with the bow's articulation and carries continuous vibrato, a deliberate wobble of the fundamental by a fraction of a semitone. The ear identifies instruments from this combined fingerprint — spectrum plus envelope — so robustly that a few tens of milliseconds of a recording usually suffice. Pitch tells you which note; timbre tells you whose voice is singing it. They are independent channels of information in the same wave.
Why does a clarinet sound so different from a flute when they're both just tubes of air?

Because one tube is open at both ends and the other is effectively closed at one end, and that changes the entire harmonic recipe. A pipe open at both ends supports a full series — fundamental, 2×, 3×, 4× — with its fundamental set by half a wavelength fitting in the tube. For a tube 0.85 meters long:

About 201.8 Hz, with all harmonics present. Close one end — the clarinet's reed end behaves as a closed end — and the tube fits only a quarter wavelength, so the fundamental drops an octave, and only the odd harmonics (1×, 3×, 5×) can resonate:

About 100.9 Hz for the same physical length. That missing-even-harmonics recipe is the clarinet's hollow, woody color, and it has a famous consequence: when a clarinetist overblows, the note jumps not to the octave but to the twelfth (the third harmonic), because the second harmonic simply isn't in the tube's vocabulary. (Real pipes need a small end correction — the wave extends slightly beyond the opening — so actual instruments run a touch flat of these tidy figures.)
Why can't you tune a drum to a clear note the way you can a guitar string?

Because a membrane's overtones refuse to form a harmonic series. A string is one-dimensional, and its modes fall at exact integer multiples — 1, 2, 3, 4 — which the ear fuses into a single definite pitch. A circular drumhead is two-dimensional, and its vibration modes are set by Bessel functions, whose roots are not integers: the first few modes of an ideal membrane sit at ratios near 1.00, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65 relative to the lowest. Those inharmonic partials do not fuse into one pitch; the ear hears a thump with a vague tonal center — you can tell a big drum from a small one, but humming 'the drum's note' is slippery. Drummers and makers fight back with physics. The timpani comes closest to pitched: its kettle of trapped air loads the membrane and shifts some modes into a near-harmonic relationship (roughly 1 : 1.5 : 2), enough for the ear to settle on a pitch and for orchestras to write actual notes for it. Tabla makers load the head with a weighted spot to align modes. But a plain snare or tom keeps its inharmonic signature — which is not a defect. The brain uses exactly that pitchlessness to classify drums as percussion, a rhythm voice rather than a melody voice.
Why does the bass in my room boom in the corners and disappear in the middle of the couch?

Because at low frequencies your room is not a space, it is a resonant box, and it has standing waves. A room dimension supports a standing wave when it equals half a wavelength — the wave reflects back on itself and locks into fixed zones of pressure (antinodes, always at the walls) and stillness (nodes). For a room 4.2 meters long, the lowest axial mode sits at:
About 40.8 Hz, and its multiples follow — the second mode:

About 81.7 Hz. Play a 41 Hz tone and the room itself sings along at the walls and corners — where every mode has an antinode, which is why bass piles up there — while a node near the room's middle can leave the couch in a dead zone for that note. Higher frequencies have so many overlapping modes that the response smooths out into ordinary reverberation; the boom-and-vanish patchwork is a bass disease, roughly below 200–300 Hz in domestic rooms. It is also why moving your seat a meter can change the bass more than any setting on the amplifier: you are not fixing the sound, you are moving between the nodes and antinodes of your room's own instrument.
Why does blowing across a bottle make a note, and what sets the pitch?

The bottle is a Helmholtz resonator: a cavity of air acting as a spring, with the plug of air in the neck acting as a mass bouncing on it. Blow across the neck and you excite that mass-spring system at its natural frequency. The classic formula balances the neck air's inertia against the cavity's stiffness: f = (v / 2π) × √(A / (V × L)), where A is the neck's cross-section, V the cavity volume, and L the neck length. Take a one-liter bottle (V = 0.001 m³) with a neck of area 3 cm² and length 5 cm. The geometry factor:
A/(V·L) comes to 6. Putting it together with the speed of sound, 343 m/s:

About 133.7 Hz — a low musical note, in the bottle's familiar range. The formula is idealized: it ignores the end correction (the oscillating air plug effectively extends a bit beyond the neck at both ends, which lowers the true pitch somewhat) and treats the walls as rigid. Its predictions are still musically useful: drink some water — shrinking V — and the pitch rises, exactly as every bottle-blowing child discovers; a longer or narrower neck lowers it. The same physics, scaled up, is behind ported loudspeaker cabinets and the thump of a car cabin with one window cracked open at speed.
I sang a note near a piano with the pedal down and the piano seemed to sing back. Was that real?

Completely real — it is called sympathetic resonance, and it is one of the cleanest demonstrations that resonance is selective. With the sustain pedal down, every piano string is undamped and free to vibrate. Your voice is a stack of harmonics. Any string whose fundamental or harmonics match a component of your voice gets pushed, cycle after cycle, by exactly timed pressure nudges — each tiny, but arriving in rhythm with the string's own natural period, so they accumulate the way well-timed pushes accumulate on a swing. Strings tuned to other notes receive the same air pressure but at the wrong rhythm; their pushes cancel out over time and they stay silent. So the piano answers you in a chord assembled from your own harmonics — sing an A and the A strings and their harmonic relatives (E, C♯ in higher octaves) shimmer back. Sing into an open guitar or hold a vibrating tuning fork against a table and the same selection happens: the table resonates broadly and gets louder; the piano resonates narrowly and gets musical. Resonance is not just amplification — it is amplification with an opinion about frequency, and that opinion is what your ear exploits in the cochlea, where the basilar membrane performs the same trick in reverse.
Didn't the Tacoma Narrows bridge collapse because of resonance, like a wine glass shattering from a note?

That is the textbook story, and it is mostly wrong — a case where the honest answer is more interesting. The wine-glass picture is forced resonance: an external rhythm matching a natural frequency, pumping energy in cycle after cycle. The 1940 Tacoma Narrows collapse looked similar on film — the deck twisting in growing oscillations — but the wind that day was blowing fairly steadily, not pulsing at the bridge's frequency. The modern understanding is aeroelastic flutter: the deck's own motion through the air changed the aerodynamic forces on it in a way that fed energy into the twisting — the structure was, in effect, extracting energy from a steady wind because of how its movement reshaped the airflow, a self-excited oscillation rather than a driven one. The distinction matters practically: you fix forced resonance by detuning or damping, but flutter demands changing the aerodynamic shape, which is why modern bridge decks are streamlined, slotted, and tested in wind tunnels. A kernel of the legend is true — the bridge did have an undamped torsional mode ready to be excited, and earlier oscillations that day were closer to a vortex-driven resonance. But 'the wind matched its frequency like a singer matching a glass' survives because it is tidy, not because it is accurate. It is a good reminder that resonance is a family of phenomena, and the famous example often belongs to a different branch of the family.
Why are guitar frets crowded together near the body and spread out near the headstock?

Because pitch rises by ratios, and frets mark off equal ratios of the remaining string. Each semitone multiplies frequency by the twelfth root of two, so each fret leaves the string at 2^(−1/12) of its previous length:
Every fret keeps about 0.9439 — 94.39 percent — of the string that the previous fret left. The first fret on a 65-centimeter scale therefore sits this far from the nut:

About 3.6 centimeters. But the twelfth fret must halve the string exactly (the octave), and the twenty-fourth quarters it — so each successive fret is placed at 94 percent of a shrinking remainder, and the spacing shrinks geometrically toward the body. The fretboard is a logarithmic ruler you can touch: equal musical steps, equal ratios, unequal distances. It is the same logarithmic bargain your ear makes with frequency everywhere — the piano's octaves, the decibel scale, and the cochlea's own layout, where each octave of pitch occupies a roughly equal stretch of membrane. Music's mathematics is ratios all the way down, and the instruments wear the proof on their necks.
How do I change vowels when I sing? The pitch stays the same but 'ee' becomes 'ah'. What moved?

Your vocal tract is a filter, and vowels are its settings. The vocal folds produce a buzz rich in harmonics — the source, whose rate sets the pitch. That buzz then travels through the throat, mouth, and nasal passages, an irregular tube whose resonances, called formants, amplify some harmonics and suppress others. The first two formants are the vowel's fingerprint: 'ee' has a low first formant and a high second; 'ah' has a high first and a mid second; the rest of the vowel family fills in the grid between. When you slide from 'ee' to 'ah' at constant pitch, the folds keep buzzing at the same rate while your tongue, jaw, and lips reshape the tube and drag the formants to new frequencies. This source-filter split explains several party tricks of perception: you can whisper a perfectly intelligible vowel with no pitch at all (the filter still works on breath noise), a singer's words stay understandable across a huge pitch range (formants hold roughly steady while the source sweeps), and helium changes your 'voice' without touching your folds — it raises the speed of sound in the tract, shifting the formants up, while the pitch stays put, producing the famous cartoon timbre. Voice identity lives in both halves: the buzz is the instrument, the vowels are its ever-moving acoustics.
What does 'the hall has a reverb time of two seconds' actually mean, and how is that number produced?

Reverberation time — RT60 — is the time a sound takes to decay by 60 decibels after the source stops: the duration of the audible tail as countless reflections bounce around the room, losing energy at every surface. Wallace Sabine worked out the founding estimate around 1900: RT60 ≈ 0.161 × V / A, with V the room's volume in cubic meters and A its total absorption in 'sabins' (the absorption of one square meter of perfectly absorbing surface, summed over all surfaces with their coefficients). Take a concert hall of 10,000 cubic meters with 1,200 sabins of total absorption:

About 1.34 seconds — a warm, symphonic tail. The formula's honesty requires its limits: Sabine assumes a diffuse field, sound energy spread evenly, which decent halls approximate and small dead rooms violate badly (a heavily damped room decays faster than Sabine predicts, which is why refinements like Eyring's exist). It also compresses a spectrum into one number — real halls state RT60 per frequency band, because a hall can be boomy-warm in the bass and dry in the treble at once. Still, the two levers it exposes are the whole game of room design: volume lengthens the tail, absorption shortens it, and everything else is detail in service of those two.
What's the difference between an echo and reverberation? Is it just how far away the wall is?

Essentially yes — the dividing line is time, and time is distance. Your auditory system fuses arrivals that come within roughly 50 milliseconds of the direct sound into a single event (the precedence effect: early reflections just add loudness and spaciousness). A reflection arriving later than that is heard as a separate event — an echo. Fifty milliseconds of travel at the speed of sound is:
17.150000000000002 meters of path. A wall reflection travels out and back, so the wall itself needs to be roughly half that from you:

About 8.6 meters — shout across a canyon or a large empty gym and the geometry is satisfied, and you hear your voice return as a distinct copy. Reverberation is what happens below that threshold, multiplied: thousands of reflections arriving in a dense, decaying stream from surfaces at every distance, none individually distinguishable. So a small room can only ever give you reverb — no surface is far enough away — while a cliff face gives clean echoes, and a cathedral gives you both: discrete slaps from distant walls riding on a long reverberant wash. The 50-millisecond figure is an approximation (it varies with the sound's character and level), but the mechanism is exact: echo versus reverb is the auditory system sorting arrivals by delay.
Why are restaurants so loud now? It feels like it's not just the crowd.

It isn't just the crowd — it is the room, plus a feedback loop in human behavior. Two design trends did the acoustic damage. First, surfaces: the modern restaurant aesthetic favors bare concrete, glass, tile, wood, and metal — all hard, reflective materials — over the carpet, tablecloths, upholstered booths, and drapes that used to absorb sound. Absorption fell, reverberation time rose, and every voice now bounces around the room several times before dying. Second, the Lombard effect: speakers involuntarily raise their voices as background noise rises, on the order of half a decibel per decibel of added noise once the room gets loud. Put them together and you have a spiral — the reflective room keeps everyone's voice alive longer, the accumulated noise pushes every talker to speak louder, which raises the noise further. A full restaurant can sit 10–15 dB louder than its designers ever intended, with no single loud person to blame. The cruel detail is that the spiral selects against the people with the least vocal reserve and the most hearing difficulty, for whom the noise floor rose fastest. The fix is unglamorous and known — absorptive ceilings and soft surfaces, i.e., spending money on something invisible — which is why the trend persists: reverberation is free to install and expensive to remove.
How do whispering galleries work? A whisper shouldn't carry across a whole dome.

It shouldn't in open air — and in a whispering gallery it isn't traveling through open air. Two related geometries cheat the inverse-square law. In a circular or elliptical room, reflections off the curved wall keep refocusing the sound: a whisper produced at one focus of an ellipse reflects off the wall and reconverges at the other focus, the same way an elliptical mirror focuses light — famous in domed spaces like St Paul's Cathedral in London and the rotunda of the US Capitol. The second mechanism is creeping: sound launched nearly tangent to a smooth curved wall hugs the surface, reflecting again and again at shallow angles, guided around the curve with far less spreading loss than free radiation. Either way, the wall acts as a waveguide, corralling energy that would otherwise disperse into the room's volume and delivering a surprising fraction of it to one special spot. Step a meter away from the focal point and the effect collapses — which is the tell that this is geometry, not magic: the energy was always there, just spread too thin to hear. Whispering galleries are a nice existence proof that 'sound fades with distance' is really 'sound fades as it spreads,' and anything that constrains the spreading rewrites the rule.
My studio sounds echoey. Should I absorb the sound or diffuse it? Aren't they the same thing?

They are opposite treatments for different diseases, and confusing them is the most common mistake in room acoustics. Absorption removes energy: porous materials — mineral wool, heavy fabric, acoustic foam — let air oscillate inside their pores and bleed the motion off as friction, so reflections come back weaker or not at all. It shortens reverberation and tames slap and flutter echoes. Its failure mode is excess: a fully absorbed room sounds dead and oppressive, and every remaining flaw stands out. Diffusion keeps the energy but scrambles its direction: an irregular surface — bookshelf-depth variations, purpose-built diffuser panels with wells of calculated depths — reflects sound into many directions at once, breaking up the coherent reflections that cause echoes and standing coloration while preserving the room's liveliness. A concert hall wants mostly diffusion and reflection (the music needs the energy); a voice-over booth wants mostly absorption (the microphone must hear only the voice); a home studio usually wants absorption at the first-reflection points and diffusion on the rear wall. Diagnose before treating: a long decay time calls for absorption, a distinct repeated slap calls for breaking up the offending reflection path, and a room that is already quiet but 'phasey' wants diffusion. Egg boxes, incidentally, do a little diffusion and almost no absorption — and nothing at all for sound escaping to the neighbors, which is a third problem entirely (isolation), with a third cure (mass and sealing).
There's one seat in our hall where the bass drum just vanishes. Everywhere else it's fine. What's going on?

You have found an interference null — a spot where two copies of the same sound arrive exactly out of step and cancel. The bass drum reaches that seat by two paths (directly, and after one strong reflection, or from two loudspeakers), and if the path lengths differ by half a wavelength, peak meets trough and the tone subtracts itself away. For a tone at 170 Hz, the wavelength is:
About 2.02 meters, so cancellation strikes where the path difference is half of that:

Roughly 1.01 meters of extra path. Move your head half a meter and the difference changes enough to restore the drum — the nulls form a fixed three-dimensional pattern of quiet and loud shells throughout the room, different for every frequency, which is why only certain notes vanish at that seat and why the effect is worst for pure, low tones: bass wavelengths are long, so the pattern is broad enough to sit inside. At high frequencies the shells are centimeters apart and average out as you move your head. Sound engineers fight nulls by moving speakers, adding a second subwoofer at a different position (filling each other's nulls), or shifting the seats — never by turning up, since doubling the power deepens the loud and quiet spots equally. Cancellation is subtraction, and you cannot fix subtraction with addition.
How much difference do people and carpets actually make to a room's echo? Put numbers on it.
Sabine's formula makes it a simple before-and-after. Take a classroom of 200 cubic meters with hard surfaces totaling about 40 sabins of absorption:

RT60 ≈ 0.81 seconds — noticeably echoey; speech consonants smear into the tail of previous syllables. Now fill it: thirty students (each person contributes roughly half a sabin or more of absorption, depending on clothing), carpet, and some soft furnishings doubling the total absorption to about 80 sabins:

RT60 falls to about 0.4 seconds — the crisp range where speech stays intelligible. The audience effect is not a small correction: in concert halls the seated audience is often the single largest absorber in the building, which is why halls are designed and measured occupied, why a rehearsal in an empty hall sounds gloriously lush and the same seats full sound drier, and why upholstered seats are specified to absorb about as much empty as a person does occupied — an attempt to keep the room's acoustics from depending on ticket sales.
Why do symphony halls look like shoeboxes, and why is a two-second reverb considered good there but terrible in a classroom?

Because 'good acoustics' means matching the decay to the job, and the jobs are opposite. Orchestral music wants envelopment: a long reverberant tail blends the ensemble, sustains harmony through the gaps, and makes a hundred players sound like one large instrument. Reverberation times around 1.8–2.0 seconds in the mid frequencies are typical of celebrated symphonic halls (stated as the usual published range for famous rooms). The classic shoebox shape — narrow, tall, rectangular, as in Vienna's Musikverein — earns its reputation through its side walls: close lateral surfaces throw strong early reflections at listeners from the side, which the auditory system reads as spaciousness and being inside the sound. Speech wants the opposite. Intelligibility demands that each syllable's tail die before the next arrives, so classrooms and lecture spaces target roughly 0.4–0.8 seconds; at two seconds, consonants drown in the wash of preceding vowels and listeners strain. Opera sits between the two, needing words and blend at once, and opera houses run shorter reverb than symphony halls for exactly that reason. There is no universally good room — there is a decay time, an early-reflection pattern, and a purpose, and the art of hall design is fitting the first two to the third. The same two seconds that crown a Mahler symphony would fail a spelling test.
Why does an empty stairwell or parking garage make that metallic 'boing' when I clap?

That is flutter echo: a single reflection trapped bouncing between two parallel hard surfaces, arriving at your ears as a rapid series of evenly spaced repeats. In a stairwell, the clap's energy ricochets wall-to-wall or floor-to-ceiling; each round trip takes the same few tens of milliseconds, so instead of a smooth reverberant wash you hear a distinct rhythmic patter that the ear fuses into a buzzy, pitched ringing — the spacing of the repeats sets an audible tone color, hence the metallic quality. It needs three ingredients: hard surfaces (little absorption per bounce, so the train survives), parallelism (so the path repeats exactly instead of scattering), and emptiness (nothing to break the path up). Garages and stairwells have all three, which is also why they sound so dramatically lively compared with furnished rooms of the same size. The cures follow the ingredients: tilt one surface, cover one surface with absorption, or clutter the path. Recording studios are built with deliberately non-parallel walls for this reason. A useful diagnostic at home: clap once in a room and listen — a smooth decay means ordinary reverb; a distinct 'zing' or buzz after the clap means a flutter path is hiding between two parallel faces.
Acoustic panels are sold with an 'absorption coefficient.' What does 0.9 actually buy me in a room?

The coefficient α is the fraction of incident sound energy a surface swallows rather than reflecting, at a stated frequency. Sabins — the currency of Sabine's formula — are just area times coefficient. Cover 20 square meters of wall with a good broadband absorber, α = 0.9:
That wall now contributes 18 sabins. The same 20 square meters as painted concrete, α ≈ 0.05:

Just 1 sabin — an eighteen-fold difference in contribution from the same patch of wall. Two cautions keep the number honest. First, α is frequency-dependent: a thin panel that scores 0.9 in the midrange may score 0.2 in the bass, because porous absorbers only work where air moves within them, and bass wavelengths need depth — a quarter wavelength of material — to be absorbed at all. Second, coefficients above 1.0 appear in manufacturers' tables and are not fraud: the lab measurement credits edge diffraction effects, effectively counting the panel as slightly larger than it is. Read the table by frequency, budget for the bass separately, and remember the coefficient buys decay-time control inside the room — it does nothing to stop sound leaving through the wall, which is isolation, bought with mass and airtightness instead.
Humans hear 20 Hz to 20 kHz, supposedly. What do other animals hear? Give me the map.

The 20 Hz–20 kHz figure is a young, healthy human's nominal range; most adults top out well below 20 kHz. Other species stake out very different territory (all figures are typical published ranges and vary by study and individual):

- Elephant — roughly 14 Hz to 12 kHz; famous for infrasonic rumbles below human hearing that carry for kilometers through air and ground
- Human — roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz (in youth; the top end retreats with age)
- Dog — roughly 40–60 Hz to 45–60 kHz; hears well into the low ultrasound, which is why 'silent' dog whistles work
- Cat — roughly 45 Hz to 60+ kHz; tuned for the ultrasonic squeaks and rustles of rodents
- Mouse — roughly 1 kHz to 90+ kHz; much of mouse social communication is ultrasonic song
- Bats — species-dependent, commonly working between 20 kHz and 120 kHz for echolocation calls
- Dolphins — up to roughly 150 kHz in some species, among the highest-frequency hearing known in mammals

The pattern underneath the table: small heads and small prey push hearing upward (short wavelengths match small targets and small ears), while the largest animals exploit the opposite end, where long wavelengths bend around obstacles and travel far. 'Ultrasound' and 'infrasound' are defined only relative to us — they are the names we give the parts of the spectrum our own ears happen to miss.
How does a bat figure out how far away a moth is? It's just listening to its own echo, right?

Right — and the measurement is pure timing. The bat emits a call, the echo returns after a delay, and the distance is the speed of sound times the delay, divided by two because the sound makes a round trip. Suppose the echo comes back 0.12 seconds after the call:

The moth is about 20.58 meters away. Working bats deal in far smaller numbers — a moth at 2 meters returns its echo in about 12 milliseconds — and they extract much more than range from it. The echo's delay gives distance; its loudness and spectrum hint at size and texture; the flutter of wings stamps a rhythmic modulation on the echo that helps distinguish insect from leaf; and as the bat closes in, it shortens its calls and fires them faster, trading range for update rate — the 'feeding buzz' just before a catch can exceed 150 calls per second. Bats also solve a brutal self-interference problem: the outgoing call is enormously louder than the returning echo, so the ear is temporarily desensitized during emission (a middle-ear muscle contracts in step with the call — the same stapedius machinery humans have, put to a faster trade). Radar and sonar are the same invention; the bat had it first by some tens of millions of years.
How does medical ultrasound see inside the body without cutting anything open? And why the gel?

It is echolocation with the same logic as the bat's, scaled to megahertz frequencies and tissue. A transducer of piezoelectric crystal converts voltage pulses into sound pulses far above hearing — typically 2–18 MHz — and then listens with the same crystal for the returning echoes. Echoes arise wherever the sound crosses a boundary between materials of different acoustic impedance: fluid to soft tissue, tissue to bone, tissue to a gas pocket. Each echo's arrival time tells the machine the boundary's depth (sound speed in soft tissue is taken as about 1,540 m/s), its strength tells how sharp the boundary is, and sweeping the beam builds the familiar cross-section image line by line. The gel is impedance engineering, not lubricant: even a hair-thin air gap between probe and skin would reflect nearly all the sound (the air-to-tissue mismatch again), so a gel with tissue-like impedance fills the gap and lets the sound in. The frequency choice is a trade: higher frequencies have shorter wavelengths and resolve finer detail but are absorbed faster, so deep structures are imaged with lower frequencies and coarser detail. What ultrasound shows, then, is not a photograph but a map of boundaries — which is why fluid-filled structures show as clean black spaces, bone and gas block the view almost entirely, and a skilled operator is really reading an echo map. (This is the mechanism in general terms; what any particular scan can or cannot show is a question for the clinicians reading it.)
Can infrasound really make people see ghosts or feel dread? I read that a 19 Hz tone haunts a laboratory.

This deserves a careful split between what is established and what is folklore, because the famous story is better than the evidence. The story: in the 1980s, engineer Vic Tandy noticed a 'haunted' feeling in a laboratory — unease, a grey figure in peripheral vision — and traced it to a fan producing a standing wave near 19 Hz; he proposed that infrasound around that frequency resonates the eyeball and smears vision. It is a wonderful anecdote and it was published as one — a case report, not a controlled experiment, and later attempts to reproduce infrasound-induced apparitions have been mixed at best; a well-known 2003 concert experiment with added infrasound reported small increases in self-reported unusual experiences, with all the suggestibility caveats that attend such designs. What is genuinely established: intense infrasound is perceivable (as pressure, flutter, and unease) at high enough levels; natural and industrial sources — surf, wind turbines, heavy machinery, volcanoes — produce plenty of it; elephants and other animals communicate with it; and monitoring networks use it to detect distant explosions and eruptions. What remains folklore: the 'brown note' (no evidence at any tested level), infrasound as a reliable fear weapon, and single-frequency ghost machines. The honest summary is that low-frequency sound at real-world levels is mostly a nuisance-and-measurement topic, while the haunted-laboratory tale is an unreplicated anecdote that outran its evidence — worth enjoying as a story and citing as nothing more.
Why does an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes me? Compute it for me.

That drop is the Doppler effect signing its name. While the ambulance approaches, each successive wave crest is emitted from a position closer to you, so the crests bunch up: the wavelength shortens and you hear a higher frequency, f′ = f × v / (v − v_s). For an 800 Hz siren approaching at 30 m/s (about 108 km/h) with sound at 343 m/s:
You hear about 876.7 Hz. The instant it passes, the geometry flips — crests are now emitted from ever-farther positions, stretching the wavelength: f′ = f × v / (v + v_s):

About 735.7 Hz. The siren itself never changed; the roughly 140 Hz step you hear at the moment of passing is the difference between bunching and stretching, and it is why the pitch drop feels so abrupt — it is a genuine discontinuity in the received frequency, occurring in the moment the source crosses your position. The same arithmetic, run on light instead of sound, is how astronomers measure galaxies receding; run on reflected sound, it is how traffic radar and blood-flow ultrasound measure speeds.
Is the sonic boom the sound of the plane 'breaking' the sound barrier — one bang at the moment it goes supersonic?

No — and unlearning that picture explains everything people actually observe. A plane flying faster than sound drags a permanent cone of compressed air behind it, like the V-shaped wake of a boat, except conical and made of pressure. The boom is the shock front of that cone sweeping over you, a sudden pressure jump (often a double jump, nose and tail shocks, heard as a bang or a double-bang). It is not an event at the plane; it is a continuous structure the plane carries for its entire supersonic flight. Everyone along a swath of ground under the flight path hears a boom as the cone passes over them — observers miles apart hear it at different times, and the plane's crew hears nothing of it at all, since they outrun their own cone. 'Breaking the barrier' language survives from the 1940s, when aerodynamicists worried about a genuine wall of drag near Mach 1; there is a real rise in drag and buffeting in the transonic range, but no barrier and no one-time bang. So a sonic boom is less like a gunshot and more like the bow wave of a ship washing over a dock: if the ship keeps moving, the wave keeps coming, and every dock along the shore gets its splash.
Is the Doppler shift the same whether I move toward the sound or the sound moves toward me?

For sound, surprisingly, no — the air provides a reference frame, and the two cases differ slightly. If the source moves toward you at 30 m/s, it physically compresses the wavelength in the air: f′ = f × v / (v − v_s). For an 800 Hz tone:
About 876.7 Hz. If instead the source is stationary and you move toward it at 30 m/s, the wavelength in the air is unchanged; you simply plow through crests faster: f′ = f × (v + v_o) / v:

About 870 Hz — close to the first answer but not equal to it, a difference of several hertz that precision acoustics must respect. The asymmetry exists because the medium defines 'moving': a moving source changes the wave pattern itself, a moving observer only changes the rate of encountering it. Light has no medium, and relativity erases exactly this asymmetry for light — one of the quiet hints, historically, that light was not going to behave like sound. Everyday life never notices a 7 Hz discrepancy in a siren; sonar engineers, bats fine-tuning their calls, and physicists comparing the two cases notice it very much.
Why do ultrasound scanners use megahertz frequencies? What's special about that range for looking at tissue?

It is the wavelength that matters. Resolution — the smallest detail a wave can distinguish — is on the order of the wavelength, so imaging millimeter-scale anatomy needs millimeter-scale waves. In soft tissue sound travels at about 1,540 m/s. At a typical scanner frequency of 5 MHz, the wavelength is:
0.000308 meters — in millimeters:

About 0.31 mm, which is why such a probe resolves structures a few millimeters across. The trade is absorption: tissue soaks up high frequencies quickly, so a 12 MHz probe gives beautiful detail a few centimeters deep and nothing beyond, while a 3 MHz probe reaches deep organs at coarser resolution. Operators choose the frequency the way photographers choose a lens. Compare the audible world: a 5 kHz tone in air has a wavelength near 7 centimeters — a camera built from audible sound would see the world blurred to the size of a fist, which is roughly the imaging quality bats achieve, and why bats hunting millimeter insects work at 50–100 kHz, where the wavelengths shrink to a few millimeters. Frequency is chosen so the wavelength matches the size of the thing you want to see.
Why do bats use such absurdly high frequencies? Wouldn't lower calls carry farther?

They would — and that is exactly the trade the bat has refused. A wave cannot reveal detail smaller than roughly its own wavelength, so to image a moth, the wavelength must be moth-sized or smaller. A typical hunting call at 50 kHz has wavelength:

About 6.9 millimeters — the scale of the insect prey itself. Drop to 5 kHz and the wavelength balloons to nearly 7 centimeters: moths would be acoustically invisible, blurred out of existence, however far the call carried. The cost of the high frequency is severe and the bat pays it knowingly: air absorbs ultrasound rapidly, faster in dry conditions, so a bat's sonar range is only meters to a few tens of meters. The bat's whole hunting style is built around that bargain — short range, exquisite detail — and different species strike it differently: some call lower and hunt larger prey at longer range in open country; some whisper at high frequency around clutter; a few have shifted to listening for the prey's own rustling sounds instead. Lower frequencies were never rejected for carrying poorly. They were rejected for seeing poorly, and for a predator that hunts by ear in the dark, seeing is the entire job.
How can infrasound from a volcano be detected on another continent? Sound should die out long before that.

Sometimes it does — and sometimes the atmosphere itself builds it a tunnel. The atmosphere is layered, and sound bends (refracts) toward layers where it travels slower, which are the colder layers. High above the weather, in the stratosphere, temperature rises again with altitude, so sound speed rises too — and sound heading upward from a ground source can be bent back down, returning to Earth a few hundred kilometers away, then bouncing and repeating. The result is a waveguide: energy trapped between the ground and the stratospheric ceiling, spreading in two dimensions instead of three, decaying far more slowly than free radiation. Infrasound is the ideal tenant for this duct because long wavelengths are barely absorbed by air and are not scattered by weather. A large eruption or explosion injects enormous infrasonic energy, and stations thousands of kilometers away register the ducted arrivals minutes to hours later. This is not a curiosity: a global network of infrasound arrays, built to monitor the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, listens continuously, and in practice it also catalogs volcanoes, meteors, rocket launches, and severe storms. The same refraction explains smaller mysteries closer to home — distant sounds mysteriously audible on some days and not others are often the sky's layers bending sound back to earth, or refusing to.
Microphones have 'polar patterns' — cardioid, omni, figure-8. What do those actually mean in practice?

A polar pattern is a map of the directions a microphone listens to — its deafness profile, plotted around it. An omnidirectional mic hears equally in all directions: it is a pure pressure sensor, and its virtues are honesty and natural low-frequency response; its vice is that it cannot refuse anything — the room, the crowd, and the air conditioner are all invited. A cardioid (named for its heart-shaped plot) hears fully from the front, less from the sides, and almost nothing directly behind — it achieves the rejection by admitting sound to both sides of its diaphragm and letting rear arrivals cancel, which makes it position-sensitive and gives it the 'proximity effect': bring a source close and the bass swells, the broadcaster's warmth trick. A figure-8 hears front and back equally and is nearly deaf at the sides — two lobes with a null plane between them, beloved for recording two facing singers on one mic and for stereo techniques built from nulls. The pattern matters because recording is mostly the art of exclusion: the instrument you want is rarely the problem; everything else in the room is. Choosing a pattern is choosing which directions to be deaf in. And since patterns narrow at high frequencies and widen at low ones (physics again — a small mic cannot steer long wavelengths), the map is always a compromise drawn per frequency band, not a single clean shape.
What actually happens if you record a sound higher than the Nyquist frequency? Where does it 'go'?

It does not disappear — it comes back in disguise, wearing a false frequency. Sampling captures the waveform at discrete instants, and any frequency above half the sample rate is ambiguous with a lower one: the samples fit a slower wave equally well, so the system believes the slower wave. The ceiling itself, for CD-rate sampling at 44.1 kHz:
Nyquist is 22.05 kHz. Feed in a 30 kHz tone — inaudible anyway, but imagine an instrument harmonic or an ultrasonic whistle — and it folds back around the Nyquist frequency: 44.1 − 30:

It reappears at 14.1 kHz, an audible phantom tone that was never in the room. This is aliasing, the same illusion that makes wagon wheels spin backwards on film: undersampled rotation is indistinguishable from slower reverse rotation. The defense is to ensure nothing above Nyquist ever reaches the sampler — an anti-alias filter before conversion — because once folded, the impostor is mathematically inseparable from a genuine tone at that frequency. Aliasing is the deep reason sample rates are chosen with margin: the 44.1 kHz standard puts Nyquist just above the top of human hearing so the filter has a transition band to work in before the fold-back zone begins.
What does '16-bit audio' actually buy? And is 24-bit really better, or just bigger files?

Bits buy dynamic range — the distance between the quietest representable detail and the loudest undistorted peak. Each added bit doubles the number of amplitude levels and adds about 6.02 dB of range. Sixteen bits gives this many levels:
65536 steps, and a theoretical dynamic range of:
About 96.3 dB — more than the span between a quiet room and a symphony's peak, which is why 16 bits sufficed for the CD. Twenty-four bits:

About 144.5 dB of range — beyond any microphone, room, or ear in the chain. So is it pointless? For the finished product delivered to a listener, essentially yes: no listening environment offers even 96 usable decibels. For recording and production, no: the extra range is headroom, letting engineers record conservatively far below the ceiling (never clipping an unexpected peak) while the noise floor stays inaudibly deep, and giving processing — equalization, mixing, effects — room to work before rounding errors become audible. The honest summary: 24-bit is a workshop convenience, not a listening upgrade; the last several bits describe a silence quieter than any room on Earth.
Why does 'compression' mean two completely different things in audio? People keep talking past each other.

Because two unrelated technologies inherited the same word, and the collision causes endless confusion. Dynamic-range compression is about loudness contours: it automatically turns down the loud parts (or, equivalently, lets you turn up everything and holds the peaks back), squeezing the distance between whisper and shout. A compressed pop vocal sits at nearly constant level so it survives car radios and earbuds in noisy streets; an uncompressed classical recording preserves the full span and demands a quiet room. Nothing is thrown away — the wave is reshaped, not reduced. Data compression is about file size: MP3, AAC, and their kin shrink the data, and the lossy ones do it by discarding information the ear is unlikely to miss, exploiting masking — a loud tone hides quiet neighbors in frequency and time, so the quiet neighbors are never stored. (Lossless formats like FLAC compress without discarding anything, by prediction and clever packing.) The tell in any conversation: if they are talking about 'pumping,' 'glue,' or a vocal 'sitting in the mix,' it is dynamics; if they are talking about kilobits per second and artifacts, it is data.
