A streamed pop song usually wears both — data-compressed for delivery, dynamically compressed by aesthetic choice — and blaming one for the other's effects is the standard muddle.
Why do all songs on streaming services play at about the same loudness now? My old MP3s jumped all over the place.

Because the platforms quietly ended the loudness war by measuring and normalizing. Each service analyzes every track's integrated loudness — a perceptually weighted average over the whole song, expressed in LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale) — and then turns tracks up or down so they all land near a common target, commonly cited around −14 LUFS for the major streaming services, though exact targets vary by platform and setting. The consequences reshaped music production. In the CD era, mastering engineers crushed dynamics to make their track louder than the next on the radio and in the changer, because louder read as better in quick comparisons. Under normalization, a crushed master gains nothing — it is simply turned down to the same target as a dynamic one, and arrives with its transients already flattened, often sounding smaller than a master that kept its peaks. Quiet passages and dynamic range stopped being competitive disadvantages. Your old MP3s jump around because they were ripped from masters made in different loudness eras with no referee; streaming added the referee. The measurement itself is worth a nod: LUFS weights frequencies by the ear's sensitivity and gates out silences, so it tracks perceived loudness far better than peak level ever did — which is why a track can peak identically to another and still measure, and sound, much quieter.
What's physically stored on a vinyl record? And why do records crackle?

The groove is the waveform, drawn as geography. A spiral groove winds from rim to label, and its side-to-side wiggle (with vertical motion in stereo, the two channels encoded in the two groove walls at 45 degrees) is a direct analog of the audio signal: a stylus rides the groove, the wiggle vibrates the cartridge, and the vibration becomes voltage. Loud, bass-heavy passages wiggle wider — so wide that groove spacing must be managed during mastering, one reason vinyl bass is often summed toward mono. The format's physics impose honest trade-offs: the record spins at constant angular speed, so the groove passes the stylus slower near the label than at the rim, and the inner tracks have less physical room per second — high frequencies there are cramped and distort sooner, which is why sequencing a loud, bright track last on a side is asking for trouble. Mastering also applies RIAA equalization (bass cut, treble boosted on cutting, reversed on playback) to fit the wiggle into the available space and lift it above surface noise. The crackle is the surface itself: dust in the groove, tiny scratches, static discharge, and pressing imperfections, each producing a click the stylus faithfully plays. None of this is a verdict on the format — listeners who love vinyl are responding to a real, particular chain of physics, mastering choices included. But the groove holds nothing mystical: it is a waveform you can see under a microscope, with the medium's limits written into its shape.
How much data is CD-quality audio, actually? Do the math for a three-minute song.
CD audio is 44,100 samples per second, 16 bits per sample, two channels. The bit rate is the product:
1411200 bits per second — the famous 1,411 kbps. Three minutes is 180 seconds, and there are 8 bits in a byte:

31752000 bytes — about 31.75 megabytes for one song, uncompressed. That number explains the entire history of digital music distribution. In the dial-up and early-broadband era, 32 MB per song was unshippable; MP3 at 128 kbps shrinks the same song to roughly a twelfth of that by discarding masked information, and the trade built an industry. It also explains the CD's capacity: a 74-minute disc holds about 780 MB of this stream, a duration often (perhaps apocryphally) linked to fitting Beethoven's Ninth. Streaming's modern codecs claw back more — at 256 kbps a song is under 6 MB — but the reference point stays the same: the uncompressed truth of two ears' worth of 16-bit audio is 1.4 megabits every second, and every format since has been a negotiation with that figure.
Why are woofers huge and tweeters tiny? Couldn't one speaker just do everything?

A loudspeaker is an air pump, and the size of the job changes with frequency. To make a loud low note, the driver must move a large volume of air slowly — wavelength at 40 Hz is eight and a half meters, and a small cone simply cannot displace enough air per cycle without absurd excursion. Big cones move more air per millimeter of travel, so woofers are big. High frequencies pose the opposite problem: the driver must reverse direction tens of thousands of times per second, so it must be light and stiff — a large, heavy cone cannot accelerate fast enough, and worse, it stops behaving as a unit, flexing and breaking into zones that radiate independently. There is also directionality: when a driver is large compared with the wavelength it radiates, the sound beams forward instead of spreading — a woofer-sized tweeter would fire treble like a flashlight, audible only on-axis. So systems split the spectrum: a crossover hands lows to the big slow pump and highs to the small fast one, each sized to its wavelengths. The one-driver dream survives in small full-range speakers, which accept the compromise — limited bass, beaming treble — in exchange for simplicity. It is the same wavelength-matching logic as bat sonar and ultrasound probes: the transducer must be built at the scale of the waves it handles.
Why does the bass vanish from my earbuds when the fit is loose? The drivers didn't change.

Because at low frequencies, an earbud is not a speaker in a room — it is a pump pressurizing a tiny sealed cavity, and your loose fit opened a leak in the pressure vessel. Bass wavelengths are meters long; the earbud makes bass not by launching waves but by cyclically pressurizing the few cubic centimeters of your ear canal. That only works if the canal is sealed: each outward motion of the diaphragm raises the pressure, each inward motion lowers it. Break the seal and the pressure escapes through the gap as fast as the diaphragm creates it — and it escapes most easily at low frequencies, where each cycle lasts long enough for the leak to equalize the pressure. High frequencies survive because their cycles are too fast for much air to escape per cycle. This is why earbud bass is a fit specification, not just a driver specification, why foam tips that expand to seal transform the same earbuds, and why pressing your earbuds in with your fingers 'fixes' the bass: your fingers are gaskets. The same physics, scaled up, is why a subwoofer in a leaky car trunk underperforms one in a sealed cabin — bass is pressure, and pressure demands a vessel.
Recording engineers obsess over 'dynamic range.' How much does a real concert actually have, and how many bits does it need?

Measure a plausible concert honestly: the quietest passage that matters sits near 30 dB in a good hall (below that, the room's own noise takes over), and the loudest orchestral peak reaches about 110 dB. The span:
80 decibels from whisper to climax. At roughly 6.02 dB of range per bit, capturing that span needs at least:

About 13.3 bits — which is why 16-bit delivery (96 dB) genuinely covers the concert with room to spare, and why the extra bits in 24-bit recording are headroom for the engineer, not extra music for the listener. The catch hiding in the arithmetic is the listening end: play that full 80 dB span in a living room whose own noise floor is 35–40 dB, and either the quiet passages sink under the room noise or the peaks reach 115 dB and the neighbors object. This is the real-world argument for gentle dynamic-range compression in casual listening formats — not dishonesty, but translation: fitting a concert hall's span into a kitchen's. The dynamic range that matters is never the medium's alone; it is the whole chain's, from the hall's hush to your room's refrigerator hum.
Is 'noise' a physical thing? My neighbor's music is noise to me and music to him.

Your neighbor has identified the honest definition: noise is not a property of a waveform but a relationship between a sound and a listener. Physicists can describe the signal completely — spectrum, level, envelope — without the word 'noise' ever becoming decidable, because the same waveform is signal to the person who wants it and noise to the person who does not. The radio engineer's version is the same idea in uniform: signal is what carries the information you are after; noise is everything else in the channel. A few consequences follow. First, 'noise pollution' is irreducibly about unwantedness, which is why ordinances regulate levels and hours rather than attempting to define horridness. Second, some sounds are noise to nearly everyone — they carry no information anyone present wants, are loud, and are hard to ignore, with low-frequency machinery hum a perennial offender because it travels through structures and cannot be tuned out by attention. Third, the boundary moves with context: the restaurant's music is ambience at lunch and interference at a business dinner. There is one more technical use worth knowing: in audio engineering, 'noise' also names specific random signals — white, pink, brown — used as test material. Those are noise by construction, not by complaint: maximum randomness, zero information, which is precisely what makes them useful yardsticks.
Why can't I hear the quiet flute line when the brass section is playing, even though the flute is still there?

That is masking, and it is a property of the cochlea, not of attention. Remember that each frequency region of the basilar membrane reports the total motion at its place. A loud brass tone sets up a large traveling wave whose skirts spread into neighboring frequency regions, swamping the small local motion the flute would have produced there — the flute's signal is physically present in the air and in the cochlea, but it no longer produces a distinguishable change in the neural report. Masking is strongest when masker and target are close in frequency, and it spreads asymmetrically: low frequencies mask high ones far more effectively than the reverse ('upward spread of masking'), because the traveling wave's shape rises gradually toward its peak and falls steeply beyond it, so a low tone's wave washes over the high-frequency region on its way in. There is also a temporal wing: a loud sound masks quieter ones arriving just before and just after it, over tens of milliseconds. Orchestrators have exploited or fought masking for centuries — doubling a line at the octave to make it cut through, spacing chords so inner voices survive — and MP3 compression is masking turned into an algorithm: whatever the brass of the moment is hiding, the encoder declines to store. Your flute line is not being ignored. At the level of the membrane, it has temporarily ceased to exist.
How can I follow one conversation in a loud party when microphones just record mush?

You are running a separation system no microphone array matches, assembled from several tricks at once. The first is binaural: with two ears, sounds from different directions produce different timing and level patterns, and the brain exploits those differences to suppress noise arriving from elsewhere — a genuine spatial filter worth the equivalent of many decibels, which collapses the moment you listen with one ear or to a mono recording. The second is source modeling: the brain knows what a voice is — its harmonic structure, its pitch contour, the way consonants interrupt vowels — and it tracks one voice's pattern through the mush the way you track a face in a crowd, filling masked fragments from context. Familiarity helps measurably: a spouse's or friend's voice is easier to follow than a stranger's. The third is attention as gain control, actively boosting the selected stream's neural representation. Hearing aids and recorders struggle precisely because they historically captured one blended channel and had no model of the scene; even modern multi-mic systems approximate only the spatial trick. The cocktail-party effect is a reminder that hearing is not recording: the ears deliver a mixture, and an enormous amount of auditory cognition is the un-mixing — which is also why the un-mixed recording of the same party sounds so much worse than being there felt.
What is tinnitus, physically? If there's no sound, what is the person hearing?

Tinnitus is the perception of sound — ringing, buzzing, hissing — without a corresponding external sound source. The most common form is subjective tinnitus: only the hearer perceives it, and no instrument at the ear can find a vibration to match. The leading general account is that it arises within the auditory system itself rather than at its input. The auditory pathway is full of gain control — amplifiers that turn sensitivity up when input falls. When cochlear input is reduced (commonly alongside some degree of hearing change, though tinnitus also occurs with normal audiograms), central auditory circuits appear to raise their gain in compensation, and at high gain, the system's own spontaneous neural activity — its noise floor — can become audible as a phantom tone or hiss, often pitched near the region of greatest hearing change. That model explains several typical features: why tinnitus often matches the frequency of a hearing notch, why it can be masked by real sound in that band, and why it fluctuates with attention and fatigue. It is a description of mechanism in general terms only — tinnitus has multiple possible causes, a small number of them objective (real internal sounds from blood flow or muscle) or medically significant, so any individual's case is a question for their own clinician, not for a physics summary. The physics point stands on its own: a perceptual system with automatic gain can, under the wrong conditions, amplify its own silence into a signal.
White noise, pink noise, brown noise — they're all just static, aren't they? What actually differs?

They differ in how their energy is distributed across frequency, and the differences are exact. White noise has equal energy per hertz — every slice of the spectrum one hertz wide carries the same power. That sounds neutral but isn't, perceptually: octave bands double in width as they rise, so the band from 1,000 to 2,000 Hz contains ten times the bandwidth of the band from 100 to 200 Hz, and for white noise therefore ten times the energy:

A factor of 10 more energy in the top band — which is why white noise sounds bright and hissy, dominated by its top octaves. Pink noise is defined to cancel exactly that: its power density falls as 1/f, so at 1,000 Hz the density is:

0.1 of its density at 100 Hz — the fall precisely compensates the widening octaves, leaving equal energy in every octave, which the ear (a ratio instrument) hears as balanced, like steady rain. Brown noise falls twice as fast again, losing 6 dB per octave rather than pink's 3, and sounds like a deep rumble or distant waterfall. Same randomness, three different spectral slopes — and the ear's verdict on each is a direct readout of the arithmetic.
I put acoustic foam panels on my wall. Why can I still hear my neighbor, and why can he still hear me?

Because you treated absorption and expected isolation — the most common confusion in all of practical acoustics. Your foam does its real job well: inside your room, it soaks up reflections, shortening reverberation and making your own sounds die faster. But sound passing through a wall is a different journey governed by different physics. Transmission loss comes mainly from mass and airtightness: a heavy, sealed barrier is hard for a pressure wave to shake, so little energy re-radiates on the other side (the mass law — doubling a wall's mass per area buys roughly 6 dB more loss, other things equal). Foam weighs almost nothing and seals nothing; to a wave trying to cross the wall it is nearly invisible. Worse, most real-world leakage is flanking and gaps — sound traveling through door undercuts, shared ducts, floor structures, and electrical boxes — paths that bypass the treated wall entirely. So the complete taxonomy is three separate problems with three separate cures: absorption (soft, porous) for echoes inside a room; isolation (mass, sealing, decoupling) for sound crossing between rooms; and diffusion for scattering reflections without removing them. The foam was never a failure — it was the right medicine prescribed for the wrong disease, and the gap under your door is likely a bigger sound leak than the entire wall it hangs in.
People talk about 'signal-to-noise ratio' for hearing speech. What does a 10 dB SNR actually mean in plain terms?
It means the speech carries ten times the intensity of the noise. Decibels again: an SNR of 10 dB is an intensity ratio of:
10 to one. That is a comfortable listening situation — think of a clear conversation partner in a moderately quiet room. Push the noise up until the SNR reaches 20 dB and the ratio is:

100 to one — effortless. The situations that strain listeners live near and below 0 dB, where noise intensity equals or exceeds the speech: at 0 dB SNR, half the acoustic energy at your ear is noise, and understanding speech depends heavily on catching the loud fragments and reconstructing the rest from context — which is why such listening is exhausting even when the words are technically audible, and why it is disproportionately hard for anyone whose auditory system has less redundancy to spare, including many hearing-aid users. It also explains a design rule for classrooms and announcements: the fix is rarely 'make the speech louder' in absolute terms — raising everything raises nothing relative — but improving the ratio, by quieting the room, moving the talker closer (inverse-square law working for you), or aiming the sound at the listeners instead of the walls.
Why do alarms and sirens sound so grating and weird instead of just being a loud pure tone?

Because a pure tone is easy to ignore, easy to mask, and hard to locate — three failures an alarm cannot afford. Alarm designers fight masking first: a steady tone at one frequency can be buried by machinery noise at the same frequency, so alarms warble, pulse, and sweep across a band, ensuring that some component always sticks out of whatever background spectrum the room has. They fight habituation second: the auditory system is a change detector that tunes out constants, so temporal patterns — the coded pulses that distinguish one alarm type from another — keep re-triggering attention. They fight localization physics third: pure low tones are nearly impossible to place (long wavelengths defeat the ear's level cues, and timing cues are ambiguous), so broadband, harsh, harmonically rich signals give the pinna and timing systems something to grip. The grating quality is partly deliberate roughness — amplitude fluctuation in the tens-of-hertz range is perceived as harshness and is biologically attention-grabbing. The trade-offs are real: an environment saturated with alarms breeds alarm fatigue, where the design goal inverts and everything is ignored together, a problem hospitals and control rooms study seriously. But the individual alarm's ugliness is not bad taste. It is the sound of a signal engineered against masking, habituation, and the geometry of the human head.
At my desk there's a laptop fan at 35 dB and an air conditioner at 45 dB. What's the total noise level?
Not 80 dB, and barely more than the air conditioner alone. Intensities add; decibels don't. In threshold units, the fan contributes 10^3.5 and the air conditioner 10^4.5. Their sum:
34785. Now compare that sum with the air conditioner by itself:

The total is only about 1.1 times the louder source's intensity — which on the decibel scale is roughly 45.4 dB. The fan, a full 10 dB down, adds four-tenths of a decibel. This is the same dominant-source arithmetic as the two televisions, and it governs real noise control: in a room with several sources, rankings matter more than counts, and quieting anything but the loudest source is nearly free of benefit. It also runs in reverse for measurement: if switching something on raises the room's level by less than a decibel, the thing you switched on is at least 7–10 dB quieter than the room already was — a quick field test engineers use to decide what is actually worth silencing.
Why do people say complete silence is actually unsettling? Shouldn't it be peaceful?

For most people it is, at first — and then the auditory system, deprived of input, turns its own gain up and starts presenting you with yourself. In an anechoic chamber, among the quietest places on Earth (the best-known report measurements around −20 dBA, quieter than the threshold of hearing itself), visitors consistently report hearing their heartbeat, blood moving in their ears, joints, breathing, and digestion. None of that is new sound; it is body noise that ordinary rooms mask with their 30–40 dB of ambient hush. The chamber removes the blanket. There is a second, subtler discomfort: your sense of a room's size and your own orientation leans heavily on reflections — the auditory system continuously reads the space from its echoes — and a chamber engineered to absorb everything returns no spatial information at all, which many people experience as pressure or wrongness rather than peace. Anechoic chambers exist for measurement, and sessions inside them are usually kept short by choice. The lesson loops back to the decibel scale's zero: ordinary 'silence' is not the absence of sound but a modest, familiar level of it, and the ear is built for a world that never fully shuts up. True quiet is not relaxing to an instrument designed to run on input — it is the instrument idling loud enough to hear itself.
Why do an octave and a fifth sound so 'right' together? Is it just habit?
It starts in arithmetic, not habit. The octave is the ratio 2:1 — take A at 440 Hz and its octave is 880. The fifth is the next simplest ratio, 3:2:
660 Hz — the E above that A. The fourth is 4:3:
About 586.7 Hz. And the major third is 5:4:

550 Hz. Small whole-number ratios keep winning the consonance rankings across cultures and centuries, and the reason is physical: tones in simple ratios have harmonics that coincide. The fifth's every third harmonic lands exactly on the octave-partner's harmonics, so the combined sound is periodic and fused rather than clashing. As ratios complicate — 16:15 for a semitone — coincidences vanish, near-miss harmonics beat against each other, and the ear reports roughness. Habit and culture tune the details (which intervals a tradition favors, how much roughness reads as expressive), but the bedrock preference for 2:1 and 3:2 appears in infants, in non-musicians, and in the design of instruments worldwide. The ear is a ratio detector, and simple ratios are the ones it can lock onto perfectly.
Pianos aren't tuned to those perfect ratios, are they? What's the compromise?

They are not, and the compromise is called equal temperament. The problem is real: stack twelve perfect fifths (3:2 each) and you overshoot seven perfect octaves — the circle does not close in pure ratios, so any fixed-pitch instrument must smear the error somewhere. Equal temperament's solution is radical democracy: divide the octave into twelve identical semitones, each a ratio of 2^(1/12), so every key is equally usable and equally slightly wrong. The tempered fifth is seven semitones:
2^(7/12) ≈ 1.4983, against the pure fifth's 1.5. The shortfall, as a percentage:

Only about 0.11 percent narrow — roughly 2 cents in musicians' units, where a semitone is 100. Fifths survive nearly pure. The real casualty is the major third: the tempered third runs about 14 cents wide of the pure 5:4, wide enough to produce audible beating in sustained chords, and the main reason a piano's major chords shimmer where a well-tuned choir's can lock into stillness. Singers and string players, owning instruments of continuous pitch, drift toward pure ratios in slow harmony and back toward temperament when the piano joins. The piano accepts its permanent slight impurity as the price of playing in every key without retuning — a tax of a few cents per interval, distributed with complete fairness.
What makes two notes sound consonant or dissonant? Is it in the sound or in my head?

Both, in layers. The deepest layer is mechanical and happens in the cochlea. Every musical tone brings its harmonic stack, so an interval is really two stacks interacting. When the stacks' components coincide or sit far apart, the membrane's response is orderly. When two components fall close but not equal — within the same critical band of the membrane, roughly a minor third wide in the midrange — they cannot be resolved separately and instead beat rapidly against each other, producing the sensation called roughness. That roughness is the physiological core of dissonance: a tritone's and a semitone's stacks are full of such near-collisions; the octave's and fifth's stacks are nearly collision-free. The classic Plomp–Levelt experiments mapped this: play two pure tones and sweep their separation, and perceived dissonance peaks exactly where the critical-band theory predicts, vanishing both at unison and beyond the band. On top of that bedrock, culture and exposure build a second layer — what counts as a satisfying tension, whether a major third sounds sweet or bland, whether roughness reads as pain or as spice — which is why traditions disagree about intervals whose roughness they all physically hear. The clean summary: the ear computes roughness for free and identically in everyone; the musical meaning assigned to that roughness is learned. Dissonance is a measurement; taste is an interpretation.
My phone's tiny speaker can't possibly reproduce a bass singer's low notes. Why do I still hear the right pitch?

Because pitch is not read from the fundamental alone — your auditory system reconstructs it from the spacing of the harmonics, a phenomenon called the missing fundamental or residue pitch. A voice at 100 Hz radiates harmonics at 200, 300, 400, 500 Hz and beyond. Your phone speaker reproduces the upper harmonics passably while the 100 Hz fundamental itself is barely radiated. The harmonics still arrive at the cochlea spaced exactly 100 Hz apart, and the auditory system — which seems to match incoming spectra against a harmonic template — infers the fundamental that would generate that spacing and reports pitch at 100 Hz. The note sounds thin, because the energy really is missing, but it does not sound an octave up. The effect is robust enough to be engineered: small speakers and 'psychoacoustic bass' processors deliberately strengthen the harmonics of bass notes so listeners perceive depth the hardware cannot produce, and telephone systems of the last century, which passed almost nothing below 300 Hz, remained intelligible and pitch-true on the same principle. It is a fine example of hearing as inference rather than measurement: the ear does not just register what arrived — it solves for the source that most plausibly produced what arrived, and sometimes the solution contains a frequency that was never in the air.
Is rhythm also ratios, like pitch? Or is that stretching the math metaphor?

It is genuinely the same mathematics in a slower band. Pitch ratios live at hundreds of cycles per second; rhythm ratios live at one to ten. A beat at 60 per minute is a 1 Hz pulse train. Play a pattern of three beats in the time of two — the 3:2 polyrhythm at the heart of much African, Latin, and jazz music — and you are performing the fifth's ratio, 3 against 2, with your hands instead of your ears' pitch machinery; musicians even learn it with the same 'feel' of two patterns locking into one composite cycle that repeats every six units. Subdivisions are ratios too: eighth notes halve the beat, triplets third it, swing delays the off-beats by a tunable fraction. The analogy has one honest limit: the ear does not fuse fast rhythms into a single percept the way it fuses harmonics into pitch — around 20 events per second rhythm blurs toward texture and then toward pitch itself, which is why a drum machine sped up becomes a buzz and a buzz slowed down becomes clicks. That boundary is a clue that pitch and rhythm are one system read at different speeds: periodicities the nervous system tracks as timing at the slow end and as tone at the fast end, with ratios governing the structure at both extremes.
Why does a choir of twenty sound so much bigger and warmer than one singer twenty times louder?

Because the twenty are not identical, and the imperfections are the sound. Each singer's pitch wanders by a few cents around the target, each voice starts and stops a few milliseconds off its neighbors, and each has its own vibrato rate and timbre. Summed, those micro-differences produce the chorus effect: a constantly shifting interference pattern among near-equal frequencies, with slow beats and shimmering partials that no single voice generates. The brain reads the result as size and warmth — plausibly because in nature, a sound that rich in independent micro-variation only comes from a genuinely large or distributed source. A single voice amplified twenty-fold has none of this: it is the same interference pattern, only louder, and it sounds like exactly what it is, one person through a loudspeaker. Recording engineers fake the choir with the recipe the choir embodies — double-tracking the same singer (two takes never match perfectly) or electronic chorus units that sum slightly detuned, slightly delayed copies. There is a real trade being made: the section gains blend and power but loses the pinpoint pitch precision a soloist can achieve, since the section's effective pitch is an average no individual may be singing. Orchestral string sections make the same bargain. Bigness, acoustically, is controlled disagreement.
Why do piano tuners say the piano's thirds 'beat'? I thought the notes were just fixed.

Because a string's harmonics are exact, and equal temperament is not — and where they disagree, beats testify. Take the lowest C string on a big piano, fundamental near 65.4 Hz. Its fifth harmonic is:

327 Hz. That fifth harmonic is exactly two octaves and a pure major third above the fundamental — nature's 5:4 third. But the piano's own E string, tuned in equal temperament, sits near 329.63 Hz. The gap between the string's harmonic and the piano's E:

About 2.6 Hz — so when C and E sound together, that harmonic pair beats roughly two to three times per second, a slow shimmer inside the chord. Tuners do not merely tolerate this; they count such beats to set the temperament, using known beat rates at known intervals as their measuring instrument — the beats are the readout of exactly how far each interval sits from purity. A choir can slide its third down those 2.6 Hz into stillness; a piano cannot, because its third must also serve eleven other keys. The shimmer you hear in a piano's major chords is the sound of a compromise being paid, a few beats per second, forever.
Do all cultures build music on the same scales? Is the octave universal?

The octave comes as close to universal as anything in music: across documented traditions, melodies treat a tone and its double as somehow equivalent — the same note returned — and instruments and vocal ranges are organized around that equivalence, which is unsurprising given that the octave is built into the physics of every vibrating string and air column a culture might pick up. Beyond the octave, diversity blooms. The five-note pentatonic family appears independently on every inhabited continent — in East Asian, African, Celtic, and Native American traditions among others — plausibly because its intervals avoid the roughest near-collisions. But the twelve equal semitones of the modern piano are a local invention, not a law: Indonesian gamelan ensembles tune to sléndro and pélog systems that divide the octave quite differently and are tuned per-ensemble, so one orchestra's instruments literally cannot substitute for another's; Arabic and Turkish traditions use intervals foreign to the piano, including three-quarter tones; Indian classical music theorizes a 22-fold division of the octave. Care is needed with the strongest claim: octave equivalence seems rooted in perception, but even its boundaries are shaped by the harmonic sounds a culture's instruments make. The safest summary is a layered one — physics supplies the octave and the simple ratios as attractors; each culture settles into its own negotiated settlement with them, and no settlement, including ours, is the inevitable one.
My delay pedal has settings like 'dotted eighth note.' What delay time is that at 120 BPM?
It is tempo arithmetic. At 120 beats per minute, one beat — a quarter note — lasts:
0.5 seconds. An eighth note is half a beat, 0.25 s, and the dot adds half again of the note's own value: a dotted eighth is three-quarters of a beat:

0.375 seconds — 375 milliseconds. That three-against-four offset is the whole point of the setting: echoes landing on the dotted eighth interleave with the played quarter notes to weave the galloping, subdivided textures made famous by guitarists like The Edge — the delay is not repeating the rhythm, it is completing it. The general lesson travels beyond pedals: every rhythmic value is a fraction of the beat, the beat is 60/BPM seconds, and all tempo-locked effects — tremolo rates, sequencer steps, the echo spacing that makes a slapback feel 'in time' — are this one division dressed in different clothes.
Why does a piano recording played backwards sound nothing like a piano?

Because a note's identity lives in its time envelope as much as in its spectrum, and reversing the tape destroys the envelope while keeping the spectrum. A real piano note begins with a violent, noisy hammer strike — a burst rich in high harmonics — and then decays exponentially, the high partials dying fastest, the tone darkening and quieting over seconds. Your auditory system leans hard on that opening transient and decay shape to classify the source; they are the signature of 'struck string' as surely as the harmonic ladder is. Played backwards, the same energy arrives in reverse order: a long, quiet swell that brightens and grows, then cuts off abruptly at what was the attack. Every harmonic that was present is still present, but the brain's template-matching finds no natural object that crescendos for two seconds and vanishes in a click, so the sound registers as an eerie, organ-like synth pad — the auditory system honestly reporting 'unknown source.' The experiment is a clean demonstration that timbre is not a static recipe of frequencies but a recipe unfolding in time, and that recognition is inference: given an impossible history, the brain declines to name the instrument at all. It is also why electronic instruments that copy spectra but botch envelopes still sound fake to untrained ears that cannot say why.
Why does a minor chord sound 'sad' and a major chord 'happy'? Is that physics or culture?

The honest answer is: mostly culture and learning, standing on a small amount of physics — and anyone who tells you it is purely one or the other is overselling. The physics that does exist: the major triad approximates the simple ratios 4:5:6, so its notes coincide with the lower harmonics of a single complex tone — a major chord is, in a sense, one big natural sound, and its components fuse smoothly. The minor triad's ratios (roughly 10:12:15) are more complex and do not match a single harmonic series as neatly. But the emotional labels do not follow from that alone. The major-happy/minor-sad mapping is strongest in Western listeners raised on Western music; it weakens or shifts in listeners from traditions where minor-like modes carry dances and celebrations, and it strengthens in children with age and exposure, the signature of a learned association. Tempo, rhythm, timbre, and lyrics each move the emotional needle at least as much as mode does — a fast minor tune can sound exuberant and a slow major one desolate, as any film score demonstrates. There may be subtler contributions (speech prosody research notes that excited speech tends toward major-like intervals and subdued speech toward minor-like ones, which would give the association a bodily root), but that work is suggestive, not settled. File this under questions where the correct scientific posture is a genuine 'partly, and we are not sure of the proportions.'
Why do older people lose the high notes first? My grandfather hears voices fine but misses the 's' sounds.

Because the cochlea is laid out like a keyboard and the high keys take the most traffic. Recall the place map: high frequencies are processed at the base of the cochlea, right where every sound wave enters. Every sound of a lifetime — loud and quiet, high and low — travels through the basal region to reach its own place, so the base's hair cells accumulate the most mechanical wear, the most metabolic stress, and the earliest losses from noise and aging alike. The result is the characteristic slope of age-related hearing change: thresholds rise first and worst at high frequencies, often beginning in the teens and twenties at the very top (which is why teenagers can hear tones near 17 kHz that most adults cannot — the famous 'mosquito' ringtone asymmetry) and marching downward with the decades. Your grandfather's symptom is the textbook consequence: vowels carry most of speech's energy at low and mid frequencies and survive, while the consonants that carry intelligibility — s, f, th, sh — live at high frequencies and thin out, leaving speech audible but muffled, especially against background noise that masks what remains. This is general physiology, not an assessment of any one person's hearing, which varies widely and has many causes beyond age. But the geography lesson is durable: in the cochlea, location is destiny, and the front door wears out first.
Why can I hear a distant train or highway on some nights and not others, when nothing about the source changed?

Because the air itself bends sound, and its bending changes with the weather's vertical structure. Sound refracts — it curves toward regions where it travels slower, and sound travels slower in colder air. On a clear, calm night the ground radiates its heat away and the lowest air becomes colder than the air above it: a temperature inversion. Sound heading upward from the distant highway enters warmer, faster air aloft and bends back down to Earth, sometimes repeatedly, ducting along the surface and arriving at your ears far stronger than simple spreading would allow. On a sunny afternoon the gradient reverses — hot ground, cooler air above — and sound bends upward, away from ground-level listeners, casting an acoustic shadow that can make a nearby source oddly faint. Wind adds its own gradient (wind speed grows with altitude, so downwind sound bends down and carries, upwind sound bends up and dies). None of this requires the source to change at all, which is why 'sound carries well tonight' is a genuine meteorological observation, used informally by sailors and artillery crews long before it was formalized. The same refraction, at grander scale, is what stratospheric ducting does for infrasound between continents. Your ears, on a still cold night, are reporting the shape of the atmosphere.
Doctors measure blood flow with Doppler ultrasound, and meteorologists track storms with Doppler radar. Same trick as the ambulance siren?

The same trick, with one extra reflection. The ambulance case is a single Doppler shift: moving source, stationary listener. In the medical and radar versions, the wave makes a round trip — it travels out, reflects off a moving target (red blood cells, rain), and returns — and the shift happens twice: the target first 'receives' the wave as a moving observer, then re-emits it as a moving source. The combined shift is proportional to the target's speed along the beam, which is all the machine needs: transmit a known frequency, measure the echo's frequency offset, and out comes a velocity. Doppler ultrasound maps flow speeds across a heart valve or a vessel, with the honest limitation that it measures only the component of motion toward or away from the probe — flow crossing the beam at ninety degrees is nearly invisible to it, which is why probe angle matters so much in practice. Weather radar runs the identical arithmetic on microwaves and raindrops, producing the radial-velocity maps that reveal rotation inside storms. One equation, three careers: the siren's pitch drop, the cardiologist's flow jet, and the forecaster's tornado signature are the same physics at different frequencies, in different media, with the reflection doubling the effect.
Why do I hear the bass from my neighbor's stereo through the wall, but not the words?

Three separate mechanisms gang up on the treble and spare the bass. First, diffraction: sound bends around obstacles by an amount that depends on wavelength versus obstacle size — bass wavelengths are meters long, comparable to walls and doorways themselves, so bass flows around and through the building's geometry while the short waves of speech are shadowed and reflected into oblivion. Second, transmission: walls obey the mass law imperfectly, and their weakest performance is at low frequencies, where panels resonate and lightweight construction simply cannot muster the inertia to resist long, powerful pressure cycles; the same wall that stops speech cold may pass a bass line with only modest loss. Third, structure: bass couples into the building frame itself — through the floor the subwoofer sits on, through shared studs — and travels as vibration to re-radiate in your room, a flanking path that bypasses the wall's airborne defenses entirely. Meanwhile the consonants that make words intelligible live at 2–8 kHz, where every one of these effects reverses: easily blocked, easily absorbed, poorly conducted. What survives the journey is exactly what you report: the beat and the bass, the melody's ghost, and none of the information. Your neighbor's stereo is not louder in the bass, necessarily — it is simply that the building is a low-pass filter.
Tiny earbuds make deep bass, but a bookshelf speaker can't fill a room with it. Both move air — what's different?

Volume of air moved per cycle, and the size of the space that air must pressurize. Bass is displacement: to produce a given pressure at a low frequency, a driver must sweep a certain volume of air back and forth. An earbud's driver is millimeters across, but it works on the few cubic centimeters sealed inside your ear canal — a thimbleful of air — so a microscopic displacement pressurizes it fully, and the 'room' is so small the driver wins easily (which is also why the seal is everything: leak the pressure and the trick dies). A bookshelf speaker in a living room faces tens of cubic meters. Its modest woofer must move enough air to pressurize that volume through the whole cycle, against the room's willingness to absorb the pressure into its size; at deep bass frequencies the required displacement grows brutally as frequency falls, the small cone reaches its excursion limits, and the output rolls off. Large woofers, ports, and subwoofers are all strategies for moving more air: more cone area, more travel, or a resonator that trades bandwidth for displacement help. Headphones sidestep the entire problem by shrinking the room to a thimble. It is the same scaling law as the woofers-and-tweeters question, one level up: the transducer must match not just the wavelength but the volume it is asked to drive.
Can people really echolocate like bats? I saw a documentary about a blind man who clicks his tongue to ride a bike.

Yes — human echolocation is real, studied, and learnable, though it works at a very different scale from a bat's. The practitioner makes a sharp, broadband sound — a tongue click is ideal, a few milliseconds of wideband energy — and listens to the echoes returning from surrounding surfaces. From the echoes' timing, loudness, and spectral color, a practiced listener can judge an obstacle's distance, size, shape, and even something of its material, well enough to navigate, identify objects on a table, and yes, ride a bicycle in familiar environments. Brain-imaging studies of expert blind echolocators show the echoes being processed substantially in the visual cortex — the brain routing spatial information to the spatial machinery it has available — a striking demonstration that 'vision' circuitry is really spatial circuitry. The limits follow from the physics already covered: clicks are audible-range, so their wavelengths are centimeters to meters, giving resolution far coarser than a bat's millimeter-scale ultrasound, and the range is a few meters, not tens. It is sonar built from spare parts — a mouth click and a general-purpose brain — and it works because echolocation was never about the frequency. It is about timing echoes, and any animal that can make a sharp sound and time its return can, in principle, learn to see with it.
What is perfect pitch, really? Is it just being very good at music?

Perfect pitch — absolute pitch — is something more specific and stranger than general musicianship: the ability to name or produce a pitch with no reference, the way you name a color. Hear an arbitrary tone and say 'F♯'; be asked to sing a C and produce it cold. It is a labeling feat, not a sensitivity feat — possessors are not hearing finer gradations than other musicians, and their relative pitch (judging intervals, the actual core of musicianship) may be ordinary. The commonly cited prevalence is on the order of 1 in 10,000 in the general population, markedly higher among musicians who began training very young, and higher again among speakers of tonal languages like Mandarin and Vietnamese — an association that points to a developmental window: the trait seems to require pitch to be wired to labels during early childhood, when the brain is assigning categories to sounds, with a likely genetic contribution to who can take advantage of that window. It is also not an unmixed blessing: because the labels are absolute, a choir drifting a quarter-tone flat can be genuinely uncomfortable to a possessor, and the reference itself can drift with age, so the C of their youth slowly becomes sharp to them. Absolute pitch is best understood as a memory-and-labeling specialization — the auditory equivalent of remembering every face — valuable, rare, and largely independent of the skills that make someone musical.
Why do professional studios sound so 'dry' on recordings, while my voice memos sound like I'm in a bathroom?

Because you are hearing the room's share of the recording, and the two rooms contribute opposite amounts. Every recording captures two sounds: the direct sound from source to microphone, and the reflected sound — the room's reverberant answer, arriving later from every surface. The ratio between them is the recording's sense of space. Your bathroom is a worst case: small, and surfaced entirely in tile, glass, and porcelain — hard, reflective, and parallel — so it returns a dense, long (for its size) reverberant field with flutter, and a phone across the room captures nearly as much reflection as direct sound. A professional studio attacks the ratio from both sides: absorption and diffusion shrink the reflected share to a short, controlled decay, and the microphone is placed close to the source, where the inverse-square law makes the direct sound dominate overwhelmingly. The result is a 'dry' signal — nearly pure source — which engineers prefer because it is a blank canvas: artificial reverb can be added in any amount and flavor afterward, but a room baked into a recording can never be removed. Your voice memo's bathroom is not a defect of the phone; it is the phone faithfully reporting a room that shouts back. Singers love bathrooms for the same reason engineers avoid them: that enthusiastic reflected field flatters a voice with free loudness and blend, at the price of clarity.
Pull it all together for me: a piano's A string and its E string — show me the whole story of that fifth in numbers.

Here is the fifth, end to end. The A string sounds its fundamental at 440 Hz and a ladder of exact harmonics above it. The E string should answer a fifth higher. Nature's fifth, the pure 3:2 ratio, would put it at 660 Hz. The piano, tuned in equal temperament, places E at 440 × 2^(7/12):
The tempered E sits at 659.26 Hz. The discrepancy from the pure fifth:

Just 0.74 Hz — and that tiny gap is not silent. Sound the two strings together and the E's fundamental beats against the A's third harmonic region at roughly that sub-hertz rate, a slow breathing in the chord that tuners count to set the instrument's compromise. Everything in this batch lives inside that one interval: a ratio (3:2) from the mathematics of vibrating strings; a logarithmic ruler (the temperament divides the octave into twelve equal ratio-steps, the same log thinking as the decibel); a wave phenomenon (beats) turned into a measuring instrument; and a perceptual verdict — the fifth sounds stable and consonant because its harmonics coincide, temperament or no temperament, to within a fraction of a hertz. The piano is a treaty between arithmetic and the ear, and the beats are the treaty's text, still legible to anyone who listens slowly enough.
